# CL-OA-008 — Conflicting Documentation Source Resolution
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-OA-008 |
| Policy Title | Conflicting Documentation Source Resolution |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | OA — OASIS & Assessment Governance |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the standardized reconciliation process that authorized OASIS assessors at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. must follow when documentation from referring facilities, prior care settings, or internal records contains conflicting clinical information that affects OASIS coding decisions. Documentation conflicts are not an exception in home health — they are a routine feature of the care environment. A patient is discharged from a hospital where the discharge summary describes them as requiring moderate assistance with bed mobility, but the home health SOC nurse observes them moving in bed with minimal physical contact. The hospital's medication reconciliation list includes a medication the patient has not taken for three months. The prior home health agency's discharge summary describes a Stage 3 pressure injury on the left heel, but the SOC nurse directly observes a wound that appears consistent with a Stage 2. The prior visit note describes SpO2 of 94% on room air, but the current assessment finds SpO2 of 88%.
Each of these conflicts creates a documentation decision with clinical, coding, billing, and compliance dimensions. The wrong choice — defaulting to the external document without explaining the conflict, or ignoring the prior internal record without acknowledging the change — produces either an inaccurate OASIS response, an inadequately substantiated response, or both. The right choice requires a defined, defensible process that: identifies the conflict explicitly; applies the evidence hierarchy from CL-OA-006 to determine which source governs; documents the reconciliation process; codes the OASIS on the basis of the governing source; and initiates clinical follow-up when the conflict has patient safety or care plan implications.
This policy implements the documentation integrity requirements of 42 CFR § 484.110, the accuracy requirements of 42 CFR § 484.55(b), and the cross-verification requirement established in CL-OA-013.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All authorized OASIS assessors who encounter conflicting documentation sources during comprehensive assessments
The OASIS Quality Reviewer who identifies conflicting source issues during quality reviews
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager who provides clinical adjudication when conflicts cannot be resolved by the assessor
All clinical disciplines who may identify conflicts between documentation sources during routine visits and must report them to the assessing RN
Physicians who may need to be notified of clinically significant conflicts per Section 6.4
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 When documentation from two or more sources provides conflicting information about the same clinical finding or patient status — and that finding or status is relevant to an OASIS coding decision — the conflict shall be identified, documented, and resolved through the standardized process established in Section 6 of this policy before the OASIS response for the affected item is finalized.
4.2 Ignoring a known documentation conflict and coding from a single source without acknowledging or resolving the conflict is prohibited. Selecting the source that produces a more favorable payment outcome, without clinical justification for the selection, violates the evidence hierarchy established in CL-OA-006 and may constitute data manipulation per CO-FA-003.
4.3 The resolution of every documentation conflict affecting an OASIS coding decision shall be documented in the assessment narrative. The documentation shall identify: the conflicting sources; the nature of the conflict; the evidence hierarchy level of each source; the source selected to govern the coding decision; and the clinical reasoning supporting the selection. Conflicts resolved through clinical judgment rather than evidence hierarchy shall be documented through the clinical reasoning process per CL-OA-012.
4.4 When a documentation conflict has clinical implications beyond OASIS coding — such as a conflict between the referral diagnosis and the SOC clinical findings that suggests a new undiagnosed condition, or a conflict between the prior wound documentation and the current wound assessment that suggests clinical deterioration or improvement — the conflict shall trigger the appropriate clinical response per Section 6.4, including physician notification per CL-CP-005 when clinically indicated.
4.5 When a documentation conflict cannot be resolved by the assessing RN through application of the evidence hierarchy, the RN shall escalate to the Director of Nursing for clinical adjudication before locking the assessment. The Director of Nursing's determination represents the agency's official coding position for the affected item.
4.6 Documentation conflicts that appear systemic — occurring repeatedly across multiple patients, involving the same referring facility, or reflecting consistent discrepancies between internal records and clinical findings — shall be reported to the Director of Nursing and flagged for quality review. Systemic conflicts may indicate a population-level change in patient acuity, a facility's documentation practices, or a gap in the agency's clinical process that requires a QAPI response per QA-PG-001.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Documentation Conflict | A situation in which two or more documentation sources provide different information about the same clinical finding, patient status, diagnosis, medication, or functional ability — where the different information cannot be simultaneously accurate and where the conflict affects an OASIS coding decision or a clinical care decision. |
| External Source Conflict | A conflict between an external clinical document (hospital discharge summary, SNF records, prior HHA records, physician notes) and the assessing RN's current clinical findings or internal clinical records. |
| Internal Source Conflict | A conflict between two documents within the current Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. episode — such as a conflict between a prior visit note and the current assessment findings, or between a physician order and the plan of care medication list. |
| Clinical Deterioration Conflict | A conflict in which more recent information indicates that the patient's clinical status has declined from what was previously documented — requiring immediate clinical attention beyond OASIS coding. |
| Clinical Improvement Conflict | A conflict in which more recent information indicates that the patient's clinical status has improved from what was previously documented — potentially affecting continued eligibility or plan of care goals. |
| Irresolvable Conflict | A conflict that cannot be resolved through application of the evidence hierarchy, additional clinical assessment, or clinical reasoning — requiring Director of Nursing adjudication and, if clinically significant, physician consultation. |
| Reconciliation Documentation | The specific narrative entry in the clinical record that identifies the conflicting sources, explains the conflict, describes the resolution process, and justifies the coding decision made in light of the conflict. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Conflict Identification — Pre-Visit and During-Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assessing RN | Before each assessment visit, review all available pre-visit documentation (referral records, discharge summary, prior visit notes, medication lists) and identify any information that could conflict with clinical findings expected at the current assessment — for example, a discharge functional status description that may differ from the patient's current functional status; a wound description from a prior note; a medication list from a facility that may not reflect the patient's current home medications. Create a "conflict watch list" of items to monitor during the assessment. | Before each assessment visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assessing RN | During the assessment visit, compare direct clinical findings against the pre-visit documentation for each item on the conflict watch list. When a conflict is identified — the observed finding differs materially from the documented expectation — document both the observed finding and the prior documentation, and note the conflict in the assessment narrative. | During the assessment visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Any Clinical Discipline | Any clinician who identifies a documentation conflict during a routine visit — for example, a PT who observes functional abilities inconsistent with the plan of care goal descriptions, or an HHA who notices wound characteristics different from the prior nursing note — shall report the conflict to the assigned RN within 24 hours. Document the conflict observation in the visit note. | Within 24 hours of identification; immediate for patient safety concerns. |

### 6.2 Conflict Classification and Evidence Hierarchy Application

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assessing RN | Upon identifying a documentation conflict, classify the conflict by type: (a) External source conflict (facility document vs. current clinical findings); (b) Internal source conflict (prior visit note vs. current findings); (c) Multi-source conflict (three or more sources with no agreement). Note the evidence hierarchy level per CL-OA-006 for each conflicting source. | At the time of conflict identification. |
| 6.2.2 | Assessing RN | Apply the evidence hierarchy to determine the governing source. In all cases where the conflict involves the assessing RN's direct clinical observation at the current assessment (Level 1 or 2) versus any external or prior internal document (Level 5 or 6), the current direct observation governs. Document this determination explicitly. | At the time of conflict identification. |
| 6.2.3 | Assessing RN | When the conflict involves two sources at the same hierarchy level — for example, two prior visit notes that conflict with each other — apply the following tie-breaking rule: the more recent source governs, provided it is internally consistent and not contradicted by physical examination findings. If the more recent source is contradicted by physical findings, the physical findings govern regardless of recency. | At the time of conflict identification. |
| 6.2.4 | Assessing RN | When the conflict involves functional status described in a hospital discharge summary (Level 6) versus the assessing RN's direct SOC observation (Level 1) — which is the most common conflict type — the SOC direct observation governs categorically. This is not a judgment call subject to clinical discretion; it is a hierarchy rule. The hospital's discharge functional description reflects the patient's status at discharge from the hospital — it does not describe the patient's status at the home health SOC, which may have changed significantly. | At each SOC where this conflict is present. |

### 6.3 Conflict Documentation in the Assessment Narrative

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assessing RN | Document every material documentation conflict in the assessment narrative using the following structured format: (a) Source A: [Identify the source, its evidence level, and the information it provides about the conflicting item]; (b) Source B: [Identify the source, its evidence level, and the conflicting information]; (c) Nature of conflict: [Describe specifically how the sources differ]; (d) Resolution: [Identify the governing source per the evidence hierarchy and explain why]; (e) Coding basis: [State which source's information was used to code the OASIS response]. | In the assessment narrative; before locking. |
| 6.3.2 | Assessing RN | The reconciliation documentation shall be specific enough that a reviewer — including a CMS surveyor — can follow the assessor's reasoning and independently evaluate whether the conflict resolution was appropriate. A notation of "conflicting information noted" without describing the conflict, the sources, and the resolution does not constitute adequate reconciliation documentation. | In the assessment narrative. |
| 6.3.3 | Assessing RN | Documentation Example — Adequate Reconciliation: "Source A — Hospital discharge summary dated 7/1/2025 (Level 6 — external document): Describes patient as requiring moderate assistance for ambulation at discharge from acute care. Source B — Direct observation during current SOC visit, 7/5/2025 (Level 1 — direct observation): Patient ambulated 30 feet from the bedroom to the kitchen without physical contact assistance, using a quad cane. Required verbal cueing for foot placement on the kitchen threshold. No loss of balance observed. Nature of conflict: Discharge document describes moderate assistance; direct observation shows setup/touching assistance (verbal cue only, no physical contact). Resolution: Level 1 direct observation governs per documentation hierarchy (CL-OA-006). Four-day interval since hospital discharge; functional status may have improved. Coding basis: GG0170B coded as 04 (Supervision or Touching Assistance) based on direct observation." | As part of assessment narrative completion. |

### 6.4 Clinical Response to Conflicts with Patient Safety Implications

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assessing RN | Assess whether the documentation conflict has clinical implications beyond OASIS coding. Conflicts requiring immediate clinical action (beyond documentation) include: (a) Current clinical findings indicating a significant decline from the last documented status — suggesting clinical deterioration; (b) Current clinical findings indicating a new condition or complication not documented in the referral; (c) Medication conflicts suggesting the patient has been taking a medication differently than prescribed; (d) Wound conflicts suggesting significant progression or new wound development since the last documented assessment; (e) Vital sign conflicts suggesting instability not captured in prior documentation. | At the time of conflict identification; before the visit concludes. |
| 6.4.2 | Assessing RN | For conflicts with clinical implications: (a) Address the immediate patient safety concern at the visit; (b) Notify the physician within the timeframe required by the applicable clinical protocol (immediately for emergent findings; within 24 hours for significant changes per CL-CP-005); (c) Update the plan of care per CL-CP-002 if the conflict reflects a change in the patient's clinical status that affects care delivery; (d) Document the clinical response in the visit note separately from the OASIS reconciliation documentation. | During or immediately following the visit; physician notification per CL-CP-005 timelines. |
| 6.4.3 | Assessing RN | If the documentation conflict suggests a wound has been incorrectly staged in prior documentation — for example, if a wound previously documented as Stage 2 now appears to be a Stage 3 on direct observation — do not attempt to reconcile the conflict through staging — stage the wound accurately based on current direct observation per the NPIAP system, document the current stage with supporting clinical observations, and notify the physician within 24 hours. Do not reverse-stage a higher-stage wound to match prior documentation. | At the time of wound assessment; physician notification within 24 hours. |

### 6.5 Escalation for Irresolvable Conflicts

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Assessing RN | If a documentation conflict cannot be resolved through application of the evidence hierarchy — for example, because the assessor is genuinely uncertain whether the current clinical findings represent the patient's typical functional status or an atypical assessment-day performance — do not lock the assessment. Contact the Director of Nursing for clinical adjudication. | Before locking; within the applicable OASIS completion deadline. |
| 6.5.2 | Director of Nursing | Review the conflicting sources and the assessor's documentation. Provide clinical adjudication guidance — which source should govern and why. If additional clinical information is needed (a supplemental assessment visit, a physician consultation), direct the assessor to obtain it before locking. Document the adjudication guidance in the Director of Nursing's communication note in the patient's clinical record. | Within 24 hours of escalation; adjusted for the OASIS completion deadline. |
| 6.5.3 | Director of Nursing | If the conflict involves a clinical finding of significant concern — a potential new diagnosis, an unexpected deterioration, or a medication safety issue — contact the physician within the timeframes required by CL-CP-005. Document the physician contact, the information communicated, and the physician's response. | Within 24 hours of identifying the clinically significant conflict; immediately for emergent concerns. |

## 7. Specific Conflict Scenarios — Standardized Resolution Guidance
The following scenarios represent the most frequently occurring documentation conflicts in home health OASIS assessments at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. This table provides standardized resolution guidance. Where the guidance below conflicts with the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual, the CMS Guidance Manual governs.

| Conflict Scenario | Resolution Approach | OASIS Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hospital discharge functional status (Level 6) vs. SOC direct observation (Level 1) | SOC direct observation governs categorically. The time elapsed between hospital discharge and the SOC visit, combined with the change in environment (hospital vs. home), makes the discharge functional status an unreliable basis for SOC coding. Document the discharge status, the observed SOC status, and the resolution. | GG functional items coded from SOC observation, not discharge documentation |
| Prior home health agency wound stage (Level 6) vs. current direct wound observation (Level 1) | Current direct observation governs. Stage the wound based on what is directly observed at the current assessment. If the prior stage was higher (e.g., prior was Stage 4, current appears to be Stage 3), do not downstage based on the current observation — review the NPIAP reverse-staging rule (pressure injuries once staged at Stage 3 or 4 retain that stage designation; a healing Stage 4 is documented as "Stage 4, healing" not as Stage 3). | M1311–M1324 coded from current direct observation; reverse-staging rule applied per NPIAP/CL-SD-011 |
| Patient self-reports independence in medication management (Level 4) vs. caregiver reports patient misses doses regularly (Level 5) | Conduct a direct medication review (pill count, pill organizer inspection, patient self-administration observation) to generate Level 1/2 evidence. If Level 1/2 evidence is obtainable, it governs. If not obtainable at the current visit, apply the more conservative source (caregiver report of non-adherence) when patient safety is at risk. Document the conflict and the resolution. | M2001, M2010 coded based on medication review findings; conflict documented |
| Discharge summary lists active diagnoses not mentioned by patient (Level 6 vs. Level 4) | External documentation governs for history items — diagnoses documented by a treating physician in recent records are appropriate Level 6 evidence for the patient's diagnostic history. Verify with the patient whether the diagnosis is currently active. Document both the referral diagnosis and the patient's knowledge of the diagnosis. | Diagnosis coding in the plan of care; homebound status documentation should reflect active conditions |
| Prior visit note documents SpO2 94% on room air (Level 5); current assessment finds SpO2 88% on room air (Level 1) | Current assessment finding governs for the current time point. Treat the change as a significant clinical finding requiring physician notification per CL-SD-020 and plan of care modification assessment per CL-CP-002. The prior SpO2 is relevant context but does not override the current finding. | Current respiratory OASIS items coded from current assessment; physician notified of deterioration |
| Medication reconciliation list from hospital includes medication; patient states they never received it and has no supply at home (Level 6 vs. Level 4) | Conduct thorough medication inventory (search all medication storage locations with patient's assistance). If medication is not found and patient confirms not taking it, code medication as not currently in the patient's regimen. Document the conflict, the investigation, and the resolution. Notify physician of the discrepancy. | M2001 coded based on actual patient medication-taking behavior; M2003 triggered if physician notification is required |

| Conflict watch list from pre-visit review | Pre-visit documentation review notation | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative (pre-visit notes section) | Before each assessment visit |
| Clinical response documentation for patient safety conflicts | Physician notification notes, plan of care modification documentation | Assessing RN | EHR — Communication notes; plan of care | Per clinical protocol timelines; retained minimum 7 years |

## 9. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 9.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material documentation conflicts identified and documented in reconciliation format | Monthly OASIS audit — presence of reconciliation documentation when conflicts are apparent from record review | ≥95% of assessments with apparent conflicts containing structured reconciliation documentation |
| GG items coded from current observation when SOC occurs after hospital discharge | Audit of SOC assessments following hospital discharge — GG narrative vs. GG coding | ≥98% of post-hospital SOC GG items coded from SOC observation, not discharge summary |
| Wound stage conflicts resolved per NPIAP reverse-staging rule | Wound staging audit per CL-SD-011 | Zero instances of inappropriate reverse-staging |
| Clinically significant conflicts result in physician notification | Communication note audit for assessments with documented conflicts | ≥95% of clinically significant conflicts with documented physician notification |

### 9.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
Surveyors will identify conflicting documentation by comparing internal records — they will look at the hospital discharge functional status and compare it to the SOC GG responses. When the SOC GG responses show greater functional independence than the discharge summary would suggest, a well-trained surveyor will look for the reconciliation documentation that explains the discrepancy. The absence of reconciliation documentation for an apparent conflict is not a compliance deficiency by itself — but it creates an interpretive problem that the agency must resolve on-the-spot during the survey. If the reconciliation is not in the record, the surveyor may conclude that the assessor simply ignored the prior documentation rather than evaluating it and making a clinical judgment.
### 9.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No pre-visit documentation review — conflicts first identified during the visit without structured reconciliation process | Unresolved conflicts resulting in inconsistent OASIS responses | Mandate pre-visit documentation review and conflict watch list as part of the assessment preparation process |
| Assessor codes from hospital discharge summary because "it was recent" without recognizing that post-discharge functional status may differ | GG items coded based on Level 6 source; potential upcoding | Train all assessors that temporal recency of an external document does not override the hierarchy; Level 1 governs regardless of how recent the Level 6 source is |
| Wound conflict between prior stage and current observation not reconciled — prior stage retained | OASIS wound accuracy failure; quality measure distortion; potential understatement of current wound severity | Annual wound staging competency includes conflict reconciliation scenarios; OASIS Quality Reviewer specifically audits wound conflicts at RECERT |

# CL-OA-009 — Point-in-Time Assessment at Start of Care
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-OA-009 |
| Policy Title | Point-in-Time Assessment at Start of Care |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | OA — OASIS & Assessment Governance |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy requires that all SOC and ROC OASIS assessments at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. reflect the patient's clinical and functional status at the time of the actual assessment encounter — not at the time of discharge from the referring facility, not at the time the referral was received, not as described in the hospital's discharge summary, and not as the patient's condition was documented at a prior point in the care continuum. The point-in-time principle is one of the most foundational and most frequently violated rules of OASIS data collection. Its violation is also among the most consequential: when an assessment is coded to reflect discharge status rather than SOC status, it over-represents functional impairment at the start of the episode and over-represents functional improvement at discharge — producing inflated quality measure outcomes that misrepresent the agency's clinical performance.
More significantly, coding a patient's SOC functional status from a hospital discharge summary rather than from direct clinical observation at the SOC visit frequently produces artificially high PDGM functional impairment scores — which generate higher PDGM payments. When this pattern is systematic, it constitutes the textbook definition of upcoding: claiming payment for a level of service complexity that was not present at the point of care delivery, based on documentation of a prior clinical state that no longer reflected the patient's actual status. The False Claims Act does not require intent to defraud — it requires only that a claim was submitted that the submitter knew, or should have known, was false or fraudulent. A systematic practice of coding SOC functional status from discharge summaries rather than direct observation, when the agency's assessors are trained and authorized to conduct direct observation, satisfies that standard.
This policy establishes the point-in-time assessment requirement as an explicit, non-discretionary coding rule at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. — supplementing the broader evidence hierarchy in CL-OA-006 by specifically addressing the most common and highest-risk application of that hierarchy.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all authorized OASIS assessors conducting SOC and ROC assessments, the OASIS Quality Reviewer, and the Director of Nursing. The point-in-time principle also applies at all other OASIS time points (RECERT, FU/SCIC, TRN, DC), where it is addressed in the respective time-point policies. This policy focuses specifically on the SOC and ROC context because these are the time points where the transition from a prior care setting creates the most significant risk of time-point confusion.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Every SOC and ROC OASIS assessment at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. shall reflect the patient's clinical and functional status at the time of the SOC or ROC assessment visit — the actual date the assessing RN conducted the comprehensive assessment in the patient's home. For items with defined look-back periods, the look-back is measured backward from the SOC/ROC assessment date, not from the patient's discharge date.
4.2 The patient's functional status, symptom status, clinical severity, and behavioral health status as documented in the hospital or SNF discharge summary represents the patient's status at the time of hospital or SNF discharge — not at the time of the home health SOC assessment. These are different points in time, and the patient's clinical status may have changed substantially during the interval between discharge and the SOC visit.
4.3 The common clinical changes that occur between hospital discharge and home health SOC include: functional improvement from early mobility programs initiated in the hospital; functional decline from deconditioning that occurs during the interval; medication changes at discharge that affect functional or cognitive status; wound progression or healing; pain improvement from discharge analgesics or pain regression as IV medications are transitioned to oral; and anxiety or depression that emerges in the home environment but was not apparent in the institutional setting.
4.4 The assessing RN shall conduct and document a direct clinical assessment of the patient's current functional status during the SOC or ROC visit — using direct observation, physical examination, and standardized tool administration — and shall code all OASIS items from that direct clinical assessment. The discharge documentation from the referring facility shall be used for history items (diagnosis history, surgical history, hospitalization history) but shall not substitute for direct observation of current functional status.
4.5 When a patient's direct SOC/ROC clinical assessment reveals functional abilities greater than described in the discharge summary — a patient who performs GG activities at a lower assistance level than the discharge documentation would suggest — this is not a discrepancy to be "corrected" by using the discharge documentation instead. It is expected clinical information reflecting the normal trajectory of recovery and the patient's actual status at the assessment time point. The direct observation governs.
4.6 When a patient's direct SOC/ROC clinical assessment reveals clinical deterioration or a new finding not described in the discharge summary — a new wound, a higher assistance level for mobility than documented at discharge, a new behavioral symptom — this information shall be coded from the direct observation and shall trigger appropriate clinical responses per CL-CP-002 and CL-CP-005.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Point-in-Time Assessment | The OASIS data collection principle that each assessment reflects the patient's status at the specific, defined moment of the assessment encounter — not at any prior or subsequent time point. |
| Assessment Time Point | The specific clinical event that defines when the assessment is conducted and from which all look-back periods are measured — for SOC assessments, this is the date of the first billable visit. |
| SOC Assessment Date | The date of the first billable home health visit — the date that establishes the beginning of the look-back period for all SOC OASIS items with look-back requirements. |
| ROC Assessment Date | The date of the first billable visit following a patient's return from an inpatient facility — the date that establishes the ROC look-back period. |
| Discharge Status | The patient's functional, clinical, and cognitive status as documented at the time of discharge from a hospital, SNF, or other inpatient facility. Represents a prior time point; not equivalent to SOC or ROC assessment status. |
| Look-Back Period | The CMS-defined timeframe prior to the assessment date during which clinical information is relevant to coding a specific OASIS item — measured from the SOC/ROC assessment date, not the discharge date. Defined in detail in CL-OA-010. |
| Status Drift | The clinical change in a patient's functional or clinical status that occurs during the interval between hospital discharge and the home health SOC assessment visit. A normal feature of post-acute care transitions; must be captured through direct SOC assessment rather than assumed from discharge documentation. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Pre-Visit Preparation — Point-in-Time Orientation

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assessing RN | Before each SOC or ROC visit, review the available referral documentation to understand the patient's clinical history, but do not use this review to pre-populate any functional or clinical severity OASIS responses. Pre-visit documentation serves the purpose of clinical preparation — identifying which assessments to perform, which standardized tools to administer, which conditions to evaluate — not the purpose of OASIS pre-coding. | Before the assessment visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assessing RN | Note the interval between the patient's hospital or SNF discharge date and the SOC/ROC assessment date. Intervals greater than 48 hours represent a meaningful "status drift" window — clinical conditions may have changed substantially. Document the interval in the assessment narrative. | Before or at the beginning of the assessment visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assessing RN | Remind yourself of the point-in-time principle before beginning the assessment: you are assessing the patient's status today, in this home, at this moment in time. You are not confirming the hospital's assessment findings. You are not extending the hospital stay's clinical picture into the home. You are conducting an independent, original clinical assessment. | Before beginning the assessment. |

### 6.2 Assessment Execution — Direct Current-Status Evaluation

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assessing RN | For every GG functional item applicable to the SOC OASIS, ask the patient to perform the activity during the assessment visit. Observe the performance. Code from the observation. If the patient's performance demonstrates greater independence than the discharge documentation suggested, code the greater independence. If the patient's performance demonstrates greater dependence than the discharge documentation suggested, code the greater dependence. The direct observation governs in both directions. | During the assessment visit. |
| 6.2.2 | Assessing RN | For clinical severity and symptom items — respiratory status, cardiac status, pain, nutritional status, bladder and bowel function — conduct the physical examination and patient interview that generates Level 1 or 2 evidence for the current time point. Do not assume clinical stability from the discharge documentation; assess current status directly. | During the assessment visit. |
| 6.2.3 | Assessing RN | For behavioral health items — administer the BIMS and PHQ-2/PHQ-9 during the current assessment visit, regardless of what behavioral health assessments the hospital may have conducted. The point-in-time principle applies to standardized tools as well: a BIMS score from the hospital reflects the patient's cognitive status at a hospital time point. The SOC BIMS reflects the patient's cognitive status in the home environment at the SOC time point. These are not interchangeable. | During the assessment visit. |
| 6.2.4 | Assessing RN | Conduct a complete skin and wound assessment at the SOC visit by undressing all dressings. Do not code wound items from the hospital's wound documentation without direct observation. New wounds may have developed since discharge; prior wounds may have changed in stage or character; wounds documented in the hospital record may not be present at the SOC. | During the assessment visit. |
| 6.2.5 | Assessing RN | If a patient's condition makes direct observation of a specific functional activity unsafe at the current SOC visit — for example, the patient's fall risk is so high that attempting ambulation would be dangerous — document the clinical reason observation was not performed and apply the substitute evidence protocol per CL-OA-006 Section 6.1 (Level 5 evidence with clinical justification). Do not default to the discharge documentation without documenting the reason direct observation was contraindicated. | At the time of the assessment; documented within 24 hours. |

### 6.3 Documentation of Point-in-Time Status vs. Prior Status

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assessing RN | When the SOC/ROC assessment reveals a functional or clinical status that differs materially from the discharge documentation, document both: the discharge-documented status (as historical context) and the currently observed status (as the coding basis). This documentation structure provides the reconciliation narrative required by CL-OA-008 for the specific point-in-time conflict between the prior facility's documentation and the current assessment findings. | In the assessment narrative; before locking. |
| 6.3.2 | Assessing RN | When the SOC assessment reveals material functional improvement from discharge status: code from the SOC observation; document the improvement as clinically expected and consistent with post-acute recovery trajectory; include this as a positive clinical finding that may affect plan of care goal-setting; do not infer that the improvement means the patient does not qualify for home health or does not need skilled services. | In the assessment narrative. |
| 6.3.3 | Assessing RN | When the SOC assessment reveals material functional decline or new clinical findings not present in the discharge documentation: code from the SOC observation; treat the new findings as a clinical priority; notify the physician per CL-CP-005; update the plan of care per CL-CP-001 to reflect the actual clinical presentation. | At the assessment; physician notification per CL-CP-005 timelines. |

### 6.4 Look-Back Period Application — Measured from SOC/ROC Date

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assessing RN | For all OASIS items with defined look-back periods, the look-back is measured backward from the SOC or ROC assessment date — not from the hospital discharge date. If the SOC assessment is conducted on July 5 and the hospital discharge was on July 3, the 7-day look-back for applicable items covers June 28 through July 5 — including the two inpatient days immediately before discharge. If the SOC assessment is conducted on July 10, the 7-day look-back covers July 3 through July 10. See CL-OA-010 for item-specific look-back requirements. | During OASIS coding; before locking. |
| 6.4.2 | Assessing RN | When a look-back period overlaps with an inpatient stay — as is common for SOC assessments that occur within the first week following hospital discharge — events that occurred during the inpatient stay within the look-back window are included in the assessment. For example, if an item has a 14-day look-back and the patient was hospitalized for 10 of those 14 days, events from the inpatient stay are within the look-back window and may inform the coding. Document when inpatient-period information is used as part of the look-back window. | During OASIS coding. |

## 7. Quality Review Integration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.1 | OASIS Quality Reviewer | At every SOC Level 2 review per CL-OA-002, specifically verify that GG functional items are coded from SOC direct observation — not from hospital discharge documentation. Red flags that suggest discharge-based coding rather than SOC observation: (a) GG narrative language that mirrors hospital discharge summary language verbatim; (b) No observable activity description — only "per discharge summary" or "per family report"; (c) GG responses that produce the maximum functional impairment score without supporting specific observation documentation. | Within the Level 2 review timeline per CL-OA-002. |
| 7.2 | Director of Nursing | During monthly OASIS accuracy audits, include a specific analysis of SOC assessments following hospital discharge: compare the hospital discharge functional descriptions against the SOC GG responses and the SOC narrative. If GG responses align more closely with discharge summary descriptions than with SOC narrative observation descriptions, flag for assessor coaching. | Monthly. |
| 7.3 | Director of Nursing | Calculate and track the agency's average functional independence change from SOC to discharge for the patient population as a whole. An unusually large improvement — well above national benchmarks — may indicate systematic SOC functional impairment overstatement (coding from discharge summaries rather than direct observation). Report this metric to the QAPI Committee quarterly. | Quarterly; QAPI reporting. |

## 8. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Point-in-time observation documentation | Activity-specific observation descriptions for each GG item coded at SOC/ROC | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | Concurrent with OASIS; retained minimum 7 years |
| Discharge-to-SOC interval documentation | Note of the interval between discharge date and SOC assessment date | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | In the SOC assessment narrative |
| Status change documentation when SOC differs from discharge | Reconciliation notation per CL-OA-008 format | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | Before locking; retained minimum 7 years |
| Look-back period application notation | Documentation of look-back window dates when applicable | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | During OASIS coding |
| Monthly SOC post-discharge functional change analysis | Comparison of GG responses vs. discharge documentation across the monthly sample | Director of Nursing | OASIS Accuracy Dashboard; Director of Nursing supervisory file | Monthly; retained minimum 7 years |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment — Appendix A | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 9. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 9.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SOC GG items coded from direct observation, not discharge documentation | Monthly audit — GG narrative language vs. discharge summary language; narrative-OASIS alignment | ≥95% of post-hospital SOC GG items with specific SOC observation documentation in the narrative |
| BIMS administered at SOC (not inferred from hospital records) | Monthly audit of M1700 supporting documentation — BIMS component scores present | ≥98% of SOC BIMS with component-level documentation reflecting SOC administration |
| Wound assessment from direct observation at SOC | Monthly wound audit | ≥98% of SOC wound items with documented dressing removal and direct wound observation |
| Agency-level functional improvement metric (SOC-to-DC) within expected benchmark range | Quarterly QAPI analysis of OASIS-derived quality measures | Functional improvement measures within ±15% of national benchmark |

### 9.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
The most targeted question in a MAC ADR audit of a home health claim is: "What was the patient's functional status at the start of care, and how was that status determined?" When the OASIS reflects high functional impairment (which justifies a higher PDGM payment group) but the clinical narrative contains language that mirrors the hospital discharge summary — rather than describing direct SOC observation — the auditor's conclusion is that the SOC OASIS was not coded from a point-in-time assessment. This is the leading cause of PDGM payment group downgrade in ADR audits.
### 9.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assessor views SOC as confirmation of discharge assessment rather than original independent assessment | GG items coded from Level 6 instead of Level 1 evidence; potential systematic upcoding | Annual training on point-in-time principle with specific post-hospital SOC scenarios |
| Narrative description uses language copied from discharge summary | Auditors recognize institutionalized language patterns; assessment integrity concern | Director of Nursing monthly audit flags narratives with discharge-summary language patterns |
| Look-back periods calculated from discharge date instead of SOC date | Incorrect item coverage; potential undercoding or overcoding | Annual training on look-back calculation; OASIS Quality Reviewer validates look-back application at each SOC review |

# CL-OA-010 — CMS Look-Back Period Compliance for Assessment Items
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-OA-010 |
| Policy Title | CMS Look-Back Period Compliance for Assessment Items |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | OA — OASIS & Assessment Governance |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy requires that all OASIS items with CMS-defined look-back periods at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. be coded using only information falling within the specified timeframe as measured from the applicable assessment date. Look-back periods are a fundamental structural feature of the OASIS instrument. They exist because many clinically important conditions — such as falls, incontinence episodes, behavioral symptoms, pressure injury occurrence, and high-risk medication use — cannot be fully assessed through a single-point-in-time clinical examination. They require information about what has happened to the patient over a defined preceding interval. The look-back period establishes the boundary of that interval — precisely enough that two assessors evaluating the same patient at the same time, using the same clinical information, should arrive at the same response for look-back-period items.
When look-back periods are ignored — when an assessor codes a 7-day look-back item based on information from 30 days prior, or uses information from within the look-back period that was actually generated at a prior care setting rather than during the applicable home health period — the result is an OASIS response that does not accurately describe the patient at the applicable time point. This produces payment classification errors and quality measure distortions. The integrity of the entire OASIS program as a quality measurement and payment instrument depends on every agency applying look-back periods correctly and consistently.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all authorized OASIS assessors, the OASIS Quality Reviewer, and the Director of Nursing. It governs all OASIS assessment time points where look-back period items are applicable.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Every OASIS item with a CMS-defined look-back period shall be coded using only information that falls within that look-back period as measured backward from the applicable assessment date per the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual. Information outside the look-back period shall not be used as the basis for coding, regardless of its clinical relevance.
4.2 Look-back periods are measured from the assessment date — the date of the SOC visit, the ROC visit, the RECERT visit, or the FU assessment — not from any other reference point. For SOC assessments following hospital discharge, this means the look-back begins at the SOC assessment date and extends backward from that date.
4.3 When a look-back period overlaps with a prior care setting (hospital, SNF, prior home health episode), events that occurred within the look-back window at the prior care setting are included in the assessment. The setting in which an event occurred does not exclude it from the look-back window. An incontinence episode during a hospital stay that falls within the 14-day look-back of the SOC assessment date is within scope.
4.4 Information from outside the look-back period shall not be used to code look-back items, even when that information is more clinically compelling or more severely represents the patient's condition than information within the look-back window. The look-back boundary is a hard boundary.
4.5 When no information about the look-back period is available — for example, when a patient is transferred and the only functional information is from clinical records predating the look-back — the assessor shall document the limitation, apply the best available evidence within the look-back window, and use clinical reasoning documentation per CL-OA-012 to explain the coding decision.
## 5. CMS Look-Back Period Reference Table
The following table summarizes look-back periods for key OASIS-E2 items. This table is based on the current CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual. When CMS updates the Guidance Manual, this table shall be updated within 30 calendar days per CL-OA-004. In all cases, the current CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual governs over this table.

| Look-Back Period | Applicable OASIS Items (Representative) | Data Collection Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Point-in-Time (Assessment Day) | GG0130 (Self-Care — SOC/ROC), GG0170 (Mobility — SOC/ROC), M1830 (Bathing — SOC/ROC/DC), M1840–M1860 (Toileting, Transferring — SOC/ROC/DC), M1870 (Eating — SOC/ROC/DC) | Reflects the patient's performance or status at the time of the assessment encounter. Activities should be directly observed during the visit when feasible. |
| Past 24 Hours | Some clinical symptom items per OASIS-E2 Guidance | Covers the 24-hour period immediately before the assessment. Patient and caregiver report are the primary sources for the preceding hours not directly observed. |
| Past 7 Days (7-calendar-day look-back) | M1700 (Cognitive Function), M1710 (When Confused), M1720 (When Anxious), M1740 (Behavioral Symptoms), M1745 (Frequency of Disruptive Behaviors), M1800–M1870 (ADL assistance items at applicable time points), GG0130/GG0170 items at RECERT/DC | Covers the 7 calendar days prior to and including the assessment date. Patient and caregiver report supplement direct observation for the full 7-day window. |
| Past 14 Days (14-calendar-day look-back) | M1730 (Depressive Feelings — PHQ-2/PHQ-9 covers "past 2 weeks"), M2001 (Drug Regimen Review), M2010 (High-Risk Medication Education), M2020 (Management of Oral Medications), M2030 (Management of Injectable Medications) | Covers the 14 calendar days prior to and including the assessment date. PHQ-2/PHQ-9 use the phrase "past 2 weeks" — this is equivalent to the 14-day look-back. |
| Since the Last Home Health SOC or RECERT | M1311 (Pressure Injury — number) | Tracks events or conditions since the start of the current certification period or since the last SOC if no prior certification occurred. |
| During the Current Certification Period | Certain wound-tracking and outcome items | Reflects cumulative status across the certification period. |
| Current/Active (no look-back — present status) | M0110 (Episodic Information), M1000–M1023 (Prior Care History), M1030 (Therapies at Home), M1033–M1036 (Risk Assessment items), M1200–M1242 (Integumentary Status — current), diagnoses | Coded based on current status or current history — not limited by a look-back window. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Look-Back Period Calculation and Application

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assessing RN | Before beginning OASIS coding at each assessment time point, identify the assessment date and calculate the applicable look-back windows: (a) Assessment date minus 7 calendar days = beginning of the 7-day look-back window; (b) Assessment date minus 14 calendar days = beginning of the 14-day look-back window. Record these dates in the assessment narrative to document that the correct window was applied. | Before OASIS coding at each assessment. |
| 6.1.2 | Assessing RN | For each item with a look-back period, gather evidence from within the defined window: (a) Directly observe the patient's current status during the assessment visit; (b) Ask the patient and caregiver about occurrences within the look-back window — not "ever" or "recently" but specifically within the defined number of days; (c) Review clinical record entries (visit notes, communication notes, physician contact notes) dated within the look-back window. | During the assessment visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assessing RN | Document in the assessment narrative that the look-back period was applied: "M1700 — BIMS administered today. Patient and caregiver interviewed regarding cognitive function over the past 7 days. Review of visit notes from [date] through [assessment date] completed." This type of documentation demonstrates that the assessor consciously applied the look-back period — not just that the assessment was conducted. | In the assessment narrative. |
| 6.1.4 | Assessing RN | When asking patients or caregivers about look-back period occurrences, use time-anchored questions: "In the past 7 days — that's since [specific date] — has there been any time when [the patient] seemed confused or disoriented?" or "In the past 2 weeks, have you noticed [the patient] feeling down or depressed on more days than not?" Time-anchored questioning produces more accurate recall than open-ended questions and demonstrates adherence to the look-back window. | During the patient and caregiver interview portion of the assessment. |
| 6.1.5 | Assessing RN | When information within the look-back window is limited — because the patient was recently discharged from a facility and has been home for fewer days than the look-back window covers — include both the home-based information (since discharge) and the inpatient-period information within the look-back window. Do not limit the look-back to only the home period. Document: "Patient discharged from hospital on [date], which is [X] days before the SOC assessment date. Look-back window for 7-day items extends from [date] through [assessment date], including the period of the hospital stay." | In the assessment narrative when the look-back overlaps with a prior setting. |

### 6.2 Common Look-Back Period Application Scenarios
Scenario 1 — SOC Assessment 3 Days After Hospital Discharge:
SOC assessment date: July 10. Hospital discharge date: July 7. For items with a 7-day look-back, the window is July 3–July 10. Four of those seven days (July 3–7) occurred during the hospital stay. Incontinence episodes, behavioral symptoms, and ADL assistance levels that occurred during the hospital stay between July 3 and July 7 are within scope for the look-back items. The assessor shall ask the patient and caregiver about those hospital days, and may contact the discharging facility for information if necessary. Document: "7-day look-back for M1700 covers July 3–10. Patient hospitalized July 3–7. Patient and caregiver interviewed regarding cognitive function during both the hospital stay (July 3–7) and at home (July 7–10). Hospital nursing notes reviewed for the July 3–7 period."
Scenario 2 — RECERT Assessment at Day 58:
RECERT assessment date: October 28 (Day 58 of the certification period beginning September 1). For 7-day look-back items, the window is October 21–28. For 14-day items, the window is October 14–28. Events from earlier in the certification period (September 1–October 13) are outside the look-back window for 7 and 14-day items and shall not be used to code those items. Document: "RECERT OASIS at Day 58. 7-day look-back window: October 21–28. 14-day look-back window: October 14–28. Information from earlier in the certification period not applicable to look-back items."
Scenario 3 — FU/SCIC Assessment Following Hospitalization:
FU (SCIC) assessment date: August 15. Patient was hospitalized August 5–12 and returned home August 12. For 7-day look-back items, the window is August 8–15. Three days of this window (August 8–12) were inpatient days. The inpatient-period behavioral, functional, and clinical information from August 8–12 is within scope for the look-back items. Document: "7-day look-back for FU OASIS: August 8–15. Patient hospitalized August 5–12. August 8–12 falls within the look-back window. Hospital records and patient/caregiver report used for the inpatient portion of the window."
## 7. Look-Back Period Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Look-back window dates documented in assessment narrative | Explicit look-back window dates for each applicable item category | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | Before OASIS coding; retained minimum 7 years |
| Time-anchored patient/caregiver interview documentation | Interview questions and responses with look-back period specified | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | During assessment; documented within 24 hours |
| Look-back window overlap with prior care setting documentation | Specific notation when look-back includes inpatient or prior care setting days | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | In the assessment narrative |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment — Appendix A | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Look-back period window dates documented in assessment narrative | Monthly OASIS audit | ≥90% of assessments with look-back items having documented window dates |
| Time-anchored interview questions used for look-back items | Supervisory observation during assessments; documentation review | ≥95% of observed assessments using time-anchored questioning |
| Look-back overlap with prior settings documented and applied | Monthly audit of post-hospitalization assessments | ≥95% of SOC/FU assessments following hospitalization with look-back overlap documentation |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
Surveyors will focus on whether look-back items reflect information from the correct window. The most common finding is that assessors code behavioral and functional items based on information from the beginning of the episode (which is outside the look-back window by the time of RECERT) rather than from the RECERT look-back window. Another common finding is that assessors limit their look-back to only the home health period when a patient recently returned from a facility — missing events that occurred within the look-back window during the inpatient stay.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assessor applies look-back from discharge date rather than assessment date | Incorrect look-back window; coding errors | Annual training with look-back calculation exercises; OASIS Quality Reviewer validates look-back documentation at each review |
| Look-back limited to home health period only — excludes inpatient events within the window | Undercoding of events that occurred during the inpatient portion of the look-back | Specific training scenario on post-hospitalization look-back overlap; assessment narrative documentation requirement |
| PHQ-2/PHQ-9 administered as "past 2 weeks" but patient has only been home 3 days | 11 days of the look-back are at the prior facility — inpatient events within the window are still in scope | Annual training covers PHQ look-back in the post-hospitalization context |

# CL-OA-011 — Standardized Assessment Tool Administration and Validity
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-OA-011 |
| Policy Title | Standardized Assessment Tool Administration and Validity |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | OA — OASIS & Assessment Governance |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy requires that all CMS-mandated standardized assessment tools — including the BIMS, PHQ-2/PHQ-9, and MAHC-10 — be administered by authorized assessors at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. in strict accordance with their validated administration protocols, and that any deviation from the validated protocol is explicitly documented with a clinical justification. Standardized assessment tools are not interchangeable clinical judgment instruments — they are psychometric instruments whose validity, reliability, and normative scoring frameworks depend entirely on administration according to the validated protocol. A BIMS administered without the word repetition component does not produce a valid BIMS score. A PHQ-9 where the assessor substitutes their own questions for the validated 9 items does not produce a valid PHQ-9 score. An abbreviated or modified tool produces data that is incomparable to the normative framework, cannot be interpreted using the validated scoring ranges, and cannot be relied upon for OASIS coding purposes.
Beyond the psychometric validity issue, there is a compliance dimension: CMS OASIS item responses that are keyed to standardized tool scores — M1700 (BIMS), M1730 and M1750 (PHQ) — are required to be derived from the validated tools, not from clinical impression or informal assessment. Coding M1700 from clinical observation of the patient's general orientation without administering the BIMS is a coding rule violation per the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual, regardless of whether the resulting response is clinically plausible.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all authorized OASIS assessors who administer standardized assessment tools, the OASIS Quality Reviewer who validates tool administration, and the Director of Nursing who oversees tool competency.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 The BIMS, PHQ-2/PHQ-9, and MAHC-10 (where applicable) shall be administered during every applicable OASIS assessment time point at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc., unless a documented clinical exception applies per Section 6.3.
4.2 Each tool shall be administered exactly as specified in its validated protocol and as required by the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual. No item shall be omitted, reworded, reordered, or supplemented with non-protocol questions. The validated administration protocol for each tool is specified in Section 6 of this policy.
4.3 Tool administration results shall be documented at the individual item level — not only as total scores — to demonstrate that each component of the tool was administered and scored individually per the validated protocol.
4.4 An OASIS response that is keyed to a standardized tool result shall not be coded from clinical impression, from prior assessment scores, from other assessors' reports, or from informal screening — unless a documented clinical exception applies per Section 6.3 and the applicable CMS guidance for the alternative pathway.
4.5 All authorized OASIS assessors shall demonstrate competency in the administration of every required standardized tool before conducting independent OASIS assessments, per CL-OA-003. Annual re-competency shall include re-demonstration of BIMS administration as a mandatory component.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Validated Protocol | The specific, published administration instructions for a standardized assessment tool — including the exact wording of items, the sequence of administration, the response option structure, the scoring methodology, and the normative interpretation framework — that constitute the tool as validated in the published research literature and as required by CMS. |
| BIMS (Brief Interview for Mental Status) | A CMS-developed standardized cognitive screening tool consisting of three components: word repetition (3 words), temporal orientation (year, month, day of week), and word recall. Scored 0–15. Required for coding M1700 when the patient can communicate. |
| PHQ-2 (Patient Health Questionnaire — 2 Item) | A validated two-question depression screening instrument requiring verbatim question reading and a 0–3 frequency response scale. Required as the initial screening for coding M1730 and M1750. |
| PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire — 9 Item) | A validated nine-question depression assessment instrument required when PHQ-2 score is ≥3 or when clinical presentation indicates depression. |
| MAHC-10 (Missouri Alliance for Home Care — 10 Item) | A validated fall risk assessment tool used in the OASIS context for applicable items. |
| Clinical Exception | A documented clinical circumstance in which the validated administration protocol cannot be completed in full — including patient refusal, communication limitations, cognitive inability, or medical instability — requiring use of an alternative pathway specified in the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual. |
| SAMS (Staff Assessment for Mental Status) | The alternative cognitive assessment pathway used when a patient cannot complete the BIMS — consisting of staff observation-based assessments of cognitive function. Used to code M1700 when BIMS cannot be administered. |

## 6. Tool Administration Protocols
### 6.1 BIMS — Brief Interview for Mental Status
Administration Requirement: At every SOC, ROC, and RECERT assessment time point where M1700 is applicable, unless a documented clinical exception requires use of the SAMS pathway.
Validated Administration Protocol:
Step 1 — Introduction (do not skip): Say to the patient: "I am going to ask you some questions about your memory and thinking. Some of these questions will be easy, and some will be harder. Let's start with a short memory test."
Step 2 — Word Repetition Component (Component A — scored 0–3): Say: "I am going to say three words, and I would like you to repeat them back to me right now, and remember them for a few minutes. The three words are: [sock], [blue], [bed]." Use these specific words. Do not substitute. Do not provide multiple repetitions — the words are stated once. Ask the patient to repeat them. Record how many of the three words the patient repeated correctly (0, 1, 2, or 3).
Step 3 — Temporal Orientation Component (Component B — scored 0–4): Ask the following three questions in sequence:
"What year is it right now?" (Score 1 if correct; 0 if incorrect)
"What month is it right now?" (Score 1 if within 5 calendar days of a new month; otherwise 0 if correct, partial credit per OASIS guidance if within 5 days of month end)
"What day of the week is it today?" (Score 1 if correct; 0 if incorrect)
Follow the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual scoring rules for the month question — specific rules apply for responses that are close to a month boundary.
Step 4 — Word Recall Component (Component C — scored 0–3): After completing the temporal orientation questions (a pause of at least several minutes from the word repetition), say: "Now, what were those three words I asked you to remember a few minutes ago?" Record how many of the three original words the patient recalls (0, 1, 2, or 3). Do not provide cues. Do not repeat the words.
Step 5 — Score Calculation: BIMS Total Score = Component A + Component B + Component C (maximum 15)

| Score Range | Cognitive Function | M1700 Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 13–15 | Cognitively Intact | Per CMS guidance — see Guidance Manual |
| 8–12 | Moderately Impaired | Per CMS guidance |
| 0–7 | Severely Impaired | Per CMS guidance |

Documentation Requirement: Document the three words used, each component score, and the total score. Example: "BIMS administered. Words: sock, blue, bed. Component A (repetition): 3/3. Component B (orientation): Year correct (1), Month correct (1), Day of week correct (1) = 3/3 total orientation. Component C (recall): 2/3 words recalled (sock, bed). BIMS Total Score: 8. Interpretation: Moderately Impaired."
### 6.2 PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 — Patient Health Questionnaire
Administration Requirement: PHQ-2 at every SOC, ROC, and RECERT assessment where M1730 is applicable. PHQ-9 when PHQ-2 total score is ≥3 or when clinical presentation indicates depression regardless of PHQ-2 score.
Validated PHQ-2 Administration Protocol:
Say to the patient: "I am going to ask you two questions about your mood over the past 2 weeks. Please answer based on how often you have been bothered by each of the following."
PHQ-2 Item 1: "Over the past 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?"
PHQ-2 Item 2: "Over the past 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?"
For each item, use the exact response scale:
"Not at all" = 0
"Several days" = 1
"More than half the days" = 2
"Nearly every day" = 3
PHQ-2 Total Score = Item 1 + Item 2 (maximum 6)
A score of ≥3 is a positive screen requiring PHQ-9 administration.
Validated PHQ-9 Administration Protocol:
Continue from PHQ-2 (use the same 2-week look-back): "Now I have some additional questions about your mood over the past 2 weeks."
Items 3 through 9 (read verbatim using the validated 9-item PHQ-9 protocol per CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual):
"Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much?"
"Feeling tired or having little energy?"
"Poor appetite or overeating?"
"Feeling bad about yourself — or that you are a failure or have let yourself or your family down?"
"Trouble concentrating on things, such as reading the newspaper or watching television?"
"Moving or speaking so slowly that other people could have noticed? Or the opposite — being so fidgety or restless that you have been moving around a lot more than usual?"
"Thoughts that you would be better off dead, or thoughts of hurting yourself in some way?"
Each item scored 0–3 using the same frequency scale as PHQ-2. PHQ-9 Total Score = Items 1–9 (maximum 27).
Item 9 Special Requirement: When a patient scores ≥1 on PHQ-9 Item 9, the suicidality assessment protocol per CL-SD-022 Section 6.5 is immediately triggered. Document the Item 9 response separately and clearly in the assessment narrative with notation that the suicidality assessment was initiated.
PHQ-9 Score Interpretation:

| Score | Severity | Clinical Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–4 | Minimal |  |
| 5–9 | Mild | Physician notification required per CL-SD-022 |
| 10–14 | Moderate | Physician notification and MSW referral required |
| 15–19 | Moderately Severe | Immediate clinical response per CL-SD-022 |
| 20–27 | Severe | Immediate clinical response per CL-SD-022 |

Documentation Requirement: Document each item response (0–3 score for each item), both the PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 total scores, the severity interpretation, and any Item 9 special action taken.
### 6.3 Clinical Exceptions — When Standardized Tools Cannot Be Administered

| Exception Type | Documentation Required | Alternative Pathway |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Patient is comatose or minimally responsive | Document patient's level of consciousness and the reason BIMS cannot be administered | Code M1700 using the SAMS (Staff Assessment for Mental Status) pathway per CMS guidance |
| Patient has severe aphasia, is non-verbal, or cannot communicate in any mutually understandable way | Document the communication limitation specifically | BIMS: Use SAMS pathway. PHQ-2/PHQ-9: Code M1730/M1750 from behavioral observation per CMS guidance |
| Patient refuses to participate in the standardized tool | Document the patient's refusal and the education provided about the tool's purpose | Code the OASIS item based on clinical observation with a notation that the tool was refused and clinical observation was substituted |
| Patient is too fatigued or medically unstable to complete the tool at the time of the assessment visit | Document the clinical status limiting participation | Attempt administration at the next visit within the OASIS completion window; if the window will close, code from the best available clinical information with documentation |
| Patient does not speak a language in which a validated translation exists | Document the language and the absence of a validated translation | Administer with a qualified interpreter for informal languages; for languages with validated translations, obtain and use the validated translation per CL-SD-022 and OP-PA-003 |

## 7. Quality Review Integration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.1 | OASIS Quality Reviewer | At every SOC Level 2 review, verify that BIMS component scores are documented (not just the total score), that the three words used are identified, and that each temporal orientation response is recorded. An assessment where only the BIMS total score is documented without components raises a protocol validity concern. | At each Level 2 review. |
| 7.2 | OASIS Quality Reviewer | Verify that PHQ-2 item scores are documented individually and that the PHQ-9 was administered when the PHQ-2 total was ≥3. A PHQ-9 not administered when PHQ-2 ≥3 is a protocol compliance failure. | At each Level 2 review. |
| 7.3 | Director of Nursing | Conduct an annual BIMS competency assessment for all authorized assessors — a direct observation of BIMS administration with a simulated patient — per CL-OA-003. Any assessor who cannot correctly administer all three BIMS components in sequence is not authorized to conduct independent OASIS assessments until remediation is completed. | Annually. |

## 8. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BIMS component scores | Component A (word repetition), Component B (orientation — year, month, day), Component C (recall), total score, and interpretation | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment module | At each applicable OASIS time point; retained minimum 7 years |
| PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 item scores | All individual item scores (0–3), total score, severity interpretation | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment module | At each applicable OASIS time point; retained minimum 7 years |
| PHQ-9 Item 9 response and safety action | Item 9 score and documentation of suicidality assessment initiation if score ≥1 | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment module; Communication notes | At each assessment; immediate action documented |
| Clinical exception documentation | Exception type, clinical reason, alternative pathway used | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | At each exception; retained minimum 7 years |

| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment — Appendix A | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 9. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 9.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BIMS administered and component scores documented at all applicable time points | Monthly OASIS audit | ≥98% of M1700 entries with component-level BIMS documentation |
| PHQ-9 administered when PHQ-2 ≥3 | Monthly audit — cross-reference PHQ-2 scores ≥3 with PHQ-9 documentation | 100% — zero positive PHQ-2 screens without PHQ-9 follow-up |
| PHQ-9 Item 9 triggers safety assessment when ≥1 | Audit of Item 9 scores — cross-reference with safety assessment documentation | 100% |
| Clinical exceptions documented with alternative pathway | Audit of assessments where tool administration was not completed | ≥95% of exceptions with documented alternative pathway |
| Annual BIMS competency assessment completed | Personnel file audit | 100% — no assessors with lapsed BIMS competency |

### 9.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
Surveyors will ask clinical staff to describe how they administer the BIMS. A common finding is that assessors describe an informal assessment of orientation (asking date, place, and person) rather than the validated BIMS protocol (word repetition + temporal orientation + word recall). The absence of the word repetition and word recall components means the assessment is not the BIMS — and M1700 coded from that assessment is coded from a non-validated instrument.
ADR auditors will specifically look for BIMS total scores without component scores — a strong indicator that the tool was not formally administered and the score was estimated. Documentation that reads "BIMS: 12" without component scores will be treated as inadequate substantiation for M1700.
### 9.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BIMS total score documented without components | Suggests informal administration; M1700 substantiation deficiency | EHR assessment template requires individual BIMS component fields; Director of Nursing reviews component documentation at monthly audit |
| PHQ-9 not administered after positive PHQ-2 | M1730/M1750 coding rule violation; behavioral health PDGM classification error | EHR workflow alert when PHQ-2 total is ≥3; OASIS Quality Reviewer validates PHQ protocol compliance at every SOC review |
| BIMS word repetition component omitted — assessor jumps directly to orientation | Validated protocol violation; BIMS score not valid without Component A | Annual BIMS competency includes direct observation of Component A administration; zero tolerance for component omission |
