## 2. Purpose
This policy mandates behavioral health screening at Start of Care and as indicated throughout the home health episode, with defined referral pathways and documentation requirements, for all patients served by Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Behavioral health conditions — primarily depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment — are among the most prevalent co-morbidities in the Medicare home health population, yet they are among the most frequently under-identified and under-addressed. The intersection of behavioral health and medical conditions in home health is profound: depression predicts medication non-adherence, slows functional recovery, increases fall risk, drives hospital readmission, and degrades quality of life. Anxiety worsens dyspnea in respiratory patients, elevates blood pressure in cardiac patients, and interferes with engagement in physical therapy. Cognitive impairment undermines the patient's ability to self-manage medications, recognize clinical deterioration, or follow safety instructions — creating compounding risk across every aspect of care. The OASIS assessment explicitly requires behavioral health screening using validated instruments — the PHQ-2/PHQ-9 for depression screening, the BIMS (Brief Interview for Mental Status) for cognitive assessment, and other standardized tools — and the accuracy of these OASIS items directly affects PDGM payment, quality measure performance, and star ratings. Incomplete or inaccurate behavioral health screening is simultaneously a clinical quality failure, a patient safety failure, and an OASIS accuracy failure. This policy ensures that every patient receives systematic, validated behavioral health screening at admission and as indicated, that clinical findings trigger appropriate and documented responses, and that patients with behavioral health needs are connected to appropriate resources through defined referral pathways.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All registered nurses (RNs) responsible for conducting OASIS assessments and behavioral health screening at SOC and applicable time points
All licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) who observe and report behavioral health indicators between RN assessment visits
All clinical disciplines who interact with patients and may identify behavioral health concerns
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager
Medical Social Workers who serve as primary community resource coordinators for behavioral health referrals
Revenue Cycle staff relying on OASIS behavioral health items for PDGM payment accuracy
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Behavioral health screening shall be conducted at SOC, at each OASIS assessment time point, and as indicated during the episode whenever a change in the patient's behavioral health status is identified by any clinical discipline. Behavioral health screening is not optional — it is a mandatory component of the comprehensive assessment and of OASIS completion.
4.2 The following validated behavioral health screening tools shall be used at the designated time points: (a) PHQ-2 (Patient Health Questionnaire — 2 item) as an initial depression screening tool at SOC, ROC, and recertification — if PHQ-2 score ≥3, proceed to PHQ-9; (b) PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire — 9 item) as a comprehensive depression assessment when PHQ-2 is positive or when clinical judgment indicates depression; (c) BIMS (Brief Interview for Mental Status) to assess cognitive function — consisting of the repetition of three words, temporal orientation (month, day, year), and recall — scored 0–15 with scores interpreted per CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual; (d) MMSE or MoCA (Mini-Mental State Examination or Montreal Cognitive Assessment) as supplementary cognitive assessment tools when clinically indicated and within the RN's scope; (e) GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder — 7 item) as an anxiety screening tool when clinical presentation suggests anxiety; (f) DAST-10 (Drug Abuse Screening Test) or AUDIT-C (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test — Consumption) when substance use disorder is a clinical concern.
4.3 The OASIS behavioral health items — including M1700 (Cognitive Function), M1710 (When Confused), M1720 (When Anxious), M1730 (Depressive Feelings), M1740 (Behaviors Demonstrated at Least Once a Week), M1745 (Frequency of Disruptive/Problematic Behaviors), M1750 (Current Level of Clinical Depression), and associated items — shall be completed accurately, using the validated tools specified in Section 4.2, and documented in a manner that is consistent with and supported by the narrative assessment documentation in the visit note per CL-OA-007.
4.4 Every patient who screens positive for depression (PHQ-2 ≥3 or PHQ-9 ≥5), anxiety (GAD-7 ≥5), cognitive impairment (BIMS score <13), or who demonstrates behavioral concerns shall receive: (a) notification of the physician within 24 hours; (b) a referral to the Medical Social Worker for psychosocial assessment per CL-SD-005; (c) documentation in the plan of care of the behavioral health finding and the planned response; (d) follow-up at each subsequent visit to monitor behavioral health status.
4.5 Safety screening shall be conducted as part of the behavioral health assessment for any patient who screens positive for depression. All patients with a PHQ-9 score ≥10, or who endorse item 9 of the PHQ-9 ("thoughts that you would be better off dead or hurting yourself"), shall be assessed for suicidality. Suicidality assessment findings shall be reported to the physician immediately, and a safety plan shall be established per Section 6.5.
4.6 Referrals for behavioral health services shall be made with the patient's and caregiver's informed understanding and consent. The clinician shall explain the reason for the referral, the type of behavioral health services being recommended, and how those services will support the patient's overall recovery. Referrals shall not be made in a manner that stigmatizes or dismisses the patient's emotional experience.
4.7 All behavioral health screening results, physician notifications, referrals, and follow-up findings shall be documented in the patient's clinical record with sufficient specificity to demonstrate that the screening was performed using a validated tool, that results were accurately recorded, and that findings triggered appropriate clinical responses.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Behavioral Health | A broad term encompassing mental health conditions (depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder) and substance use disorders (alcohol use disorder, drug use disorder), as well as behavioral manifestations of cognitive impairment. |
| PHQ-2 | The Patient Health Questionnaire — 2 item: a validated two-question depression screening tool that asks about the frequency of depressed mood and anhedonia over the past 2 weeks. A score ≥3 is a positive screen requiring PHQ-9 administration. |
| PHQ-9 | The Patient Health Questionnaire — 9 item: a validated nine-question depression assessment tool corresponding to the DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder. Scores are interpreted as: 1–4 Minimal, 5–9 Mild, 10–14 Moderate, 15–19 Moderately Severe, 20–27 Severe. |
| BIMS | The Brief Interview for Mental Status: a validated CMS-developed cognitive screening tool used in post-acute care settings to assess orientation and memory. Scored 0–15: 13–15 Cognitively Intact, 8–12 Moderately Impaired, 0–7 Severely Impaired. |
| GAD-7 | The Generalized Anxiety Disorder — 7 item scale: a validated seven-question anxiety screening and assessment tool. Scores: 5–9 Mild, 10–14 Moderate, 15–21 Severe anxiety. |
| AUDIT-C | The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test — Consumption subscale: a three-question validated alcohol misuse screening tool. |
| DAST-10 | The Drug Abuse Screening Test — 10 item: a validated self-report screening tool for drug misuse. |
| Anhedonia | The loss of interest or pleasure in activities that were previously enjoyable — one of the two core diagnostic symptoms of major depressive disorder. |
| Suicidality | The presence of suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. Ranges from passive death wish ("I would be better off dead") to active suicidal ideation with a specific plan and means. |
| Safety Plan | A structured, documented plan developed with a patient who is at risk for suicide, identifying warning signs, coping strategies, support contacts, and crisis resources. |
| Cognitive Impairment | A deficit in one or more cognitive domains (memory, attention, executive function, language, visuospatial function) that represents a decline from a previous level of function and affects daily activities. |
| Referral Pathway | A defined, documented clinical pathway for connecting a patient with a specific type of behavioral health service, including the type of service, how the referral is made, and how the outcome is tracked. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Behavioral Health Screening at SOC

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned RN | Prior to administering any behavioral health screening tool, assess the patient's ability to participate: (a) Is the patient able to communicate verbally (or in writing if non-verbal)? (b) Does the patient require an interpreter? (c) Is the patient acutely medically distressed in a way that makes screening inappropriate at this moment (severe dyspnea, acute pain, acute confusion)? If the patient cannot participate in screening at the SOC visit, document the reason, provide screening at the next visit within 5 business days, and use clinical observation to document behavioral health indicators in the interim. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned RN | Administer the PHQ-2 to all patients. Read the questions aloud and record the patient's response: "Over the past 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by: (1) Little interest or pleasure in doing things? (2) Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?" Score each item 0–3 (Not at all = 0, Several days = 1, More than half the days = 2, Nearly every day = 3). Calculate the total PHQ-2 score. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned RN | If the PHQ-2 total score is ≥3 (positive screen), immediately proceed to administer the full PHQ-9. Read all 9 questions and record responses per the validated scoring protocol. Calculate the total PHQ-9 score and record the interpretation (Minimal/Mild/Moderate/Moderately Severe/Severe). If the PHQ-2 score is <3 but clinical observation suggests depression (patient appears sad, tearful, socially withdrawn, expresses hopelessness), administer the PHQ-9 based on clinical judgment. | Immediately following PHQ-2 if positive; or as clinically indicated. |
| 6.1.4 | Assigned RN | If the patient endorses PHQ-9 item 9 (thoughts of self-harm or being better off dead) with a score ≥1, immediately follow the suicidality assessment and safety plan protocol per Section 6.5. | Immediately upon PHQ-9 item 9 endorsement. |
| 6.1.5 | Assigned RN | Administer the BIMS to assess cognitive function. The BIMS consists of three components: (a) repetition — ask the patient to repeat three words (sock, blue, bed); (b) temporal orientation — ask the patient the current day of the week, year, and month; (c) recall — after a pause, ask the patient to recall the three words. Score per the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual. Document the raw scores for each component and the total score. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.6 | Assigned RN | If the BIMS score suggests cognitive impairment (score <13), supplement with a structured clinical assessment of cognitive domains: orientation, short-term and long-term memory, attention (digit span or serial subtraction), language (naming common objects), and executive function (ability to follow multi-step commands). Document all clinical observations. | At the SOC visit when BIMS <13. |
| 6.1.7 | Assigned RN | Administer the GAD-7 if: (a) the patient self-reports anxiety; (b) clinical observation suggests anxiety (excessive worry, restlessness, difficulty relaxing, avoidance behaviors, somatic anxiety symptoms — palpitations, trembling, sweating); (c) the patient has a diagnosis of anxiety disorder. Score per the validated protocol and document the score and interpretation. | At the SOC visit when clinically indicated. |
| 6.1.8 | Assigned RN | For patients with suspected substance use concerns (history of alcohol or drug use disorder, clinical presentation suggesting acute intoxication or withdrawal, medications that suggest substance use disorder treatment), administer the AUDIT-C and/or DAST-10 per clinical judgment and physician guidance. | At the SOC visit when clinically indicated. |
| 6.1.9 | Assigned RN | Document all screening results in the clinical record using the Behavioral Health Screening Documentation Form (Appendix A), ensuring that: (a) the tool name and version are documented; (b) the individual item responses are recorded (not just the total score); (c) the total score and interpretation are documented; (d) the clinical significance of the findings is assessed and documented; (e) the planned response to the findings is documented. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.10 | Assigned RN | Ensure that all OASIS behavioral health items are coded consistently with the screening tool results and the narrative assessment documentation per CL-OA-007. | At the time of OASIS completion. |

### 6.2 Ongoing Behavioral Health Monitoring During the Episode

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | At every patient visit, screen for behavioral health changes using clinical observation: (a) Is the patient's affect congruent with their situation? (b) Has the patient's mood changed since the last visit (more withdrawn, tearful, hopeless, agitated, confused)? (c) Is the patient's sleep pattern disturbed? (d) Is the patient's appetite changed? (e) Has the patient expressed any statements suggesting hopelessness, worthlessness, or thoughts of self-harm? (f) Is the patient's cognition at baseline or declining? (g) Is the patient exhibiting new or worsening behavioral symptoms (agitation, wandering, combativeness, paranoia)? | At every visit by all disciplines. |
| 6.2.2 | Any Clinical Discipline | When a behavioral health change is identified during any visit, document the specific observation and report it to the assigned RN within 24 hours. | Within 24 hours of identification. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN | When any behavioral health change is reported or identified, conduct a focused behavioral health reassessment using the appropriate validated tool (PHQ-9 for depression, GAD-7 for anxiety, cognitive assessment for cognitive change). Document the reassessment findings and compare to the SOC baseline. | Within 48 hours of the reported change. |
| 6.2.4 | Assigned RN | Administer the PHQ-9 at each OASIS assessment time point (recertification) for all patients, regardless of the SOC screening result, to track depression status over the episode. | At each OASIS time point. |

### 6.3 Physician Notification and Plan of Care Integration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN | Notify the physician within 24 hours of any of the following behavioral health screening findings: (a) PHQ-2 ≥3 (positive depression screen); (b) PHQ-9 ≥5 (any level of depression); (c) BIMS score <8 (severely impaired cognition); (d) GAD-7 ≥10 (moderate to severe anxiety); (e) Any new or significantly worsening behavioral health finding identified during the episode. Document the physician notification, the information communicated, and the physician's response. | Within 24 hours of the finding. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | Incorporate behavioral health findings and the planned response into the plan of care per CL-CP-001, including: the specific screening results; the physician's guidance; any ordered behavioral health medications; the referral plan; and the behavioral health monitoring plan for the episode. | Within 24 hours of physician notification. |

### 6.4 Behavioral Health Referral Pathways

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assigned RN / MSW | For patients with a positive behavioral health screen, initiate referral through the following pathway, based on the finding: (a) Depression (PHQ-9 ≥5) — Mild (5–9): MSW referral for psychosocial assessment and support; physician notification; depression education; follow-up at each visit; (b) Depression (PHQ-9 ≥10) — Moderate to Severe: MSW referral; physician notification for medication consideration; referral to outpatient mental health provider or behavioral health integrated care program; follow-up at each visit; (c) Cognitive Impairment (BIMS <13): MSW referral; physician notification for further evaluation consideration (cognitive testing, neurology referral, medication review); safety assessment per RM-PS-004; caregiver education; safety planning; (d) Anxiety (GAD-7 ≥10): MSW referral; physician notification for medication consideration; anxiety management education and techniques; (e) Substance Use Concern (AUDIT-C or DAST-10 positive): MSW referral; physician notification; referral to substance use disorder treatment resources; motivational interviewing techniques. | Within 48 hours of positive screen. |
| 6.4.2 | MSW | Conduct a psychosocial assessment per CL-SD-005 for all patients referred for behavioral health concerns. The psychosocial assessment shall include: the patient's behavioral health history; current symptoms and functional impact; social support system; current and prior behavioral health treatment; willingness to engage in behavioral health services; and identification of specific community behavioral health resources available to the patient. | Within 48 hours of referral. |
| 6.4.3 | MSW / Assigned RN | Document all behavioral health referrals per CL-CP-005, including: the resource or provider referred to; the reason for referral; the date; the method; the patient's response; and any follow-up needed. For referrals to outpatient providers, document confirmation of the referral acceptance or the patient's appointment. | Within 48 hours of referral; follow-up at each subsequent visit. |

### 6.5 Suicidality Assessment and Safety Planning

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Assigned RN | When a patient endorses PHQ-9 item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead or hurting yourself) with a score ≥1, immediately conduct a structured suicidality assessment using the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) or equivalent validated tool, assessing: (a) the frequency, intensity, and duration of suicidal ideation; (b) the presence of a plan; (c) the presence of means (access to firearms, medications, or other methods); (d) history of prior suicide attempts; (e) current protective factors (reasons for living, social support, religious beliefs). | Immediately upon PHQ-9 item 9 endorsement. |
| 6.5.2 | Assigned RN | Based on the suicidality assessment, classify the risk level: (a) Low risk — passive death wish without intent or plan; no history of attempts; strong protective factors: Notify physician within 24 hours; MSW referral; increase visit frequency; safety education; document safety plan with patient; (b) Moderate risk — active suicidal ideation without specific plan; or ideation with plan but no immediate means: Notify physician within 4 hours; MSW contact same day; physician may order crisis intervention or psychiatric evaluation; document safety plan; (c) High risk — active suicidal ideation with plan and means; active intent: Call 911 immediately; do not leave the patient alone; notify physician immediately; complete incident report per RM-ER-002; stay with the patient until emergency services arrive. | Immediately upon completion of suicidality assessment. |
| 6.5.3 | Assigned RN | For patients at Low or Moderate risk, develop a written safety plan with the patient, documenting: (a) warning signs that suicidal thoughts are intensifying; (b) internal coping strategies (what the patient can do independently to manage the thoughts); (c) social contacts the patient can reach for distraction (non-crisis); (d) family members or friends who can provide support; (e) crisis resources — National Suicide Prevention Lifeline (988), Crisis Text Line (Text HOME to 741741), local crisis center phone number; (f) means restriction — discussion with the patient and caregiver about securing access to potential means (medications locked away, firearms secured). | At the visit where the suicidality assessment is completed. |
| 6.5.4 | Director of Nursing | The Director of Nursing shall be notified within 2 hours of any suicidality finding, regardless of risk level. The Director of Nursing shall ensure that appropriate clinical and administrative actions are completed, that the Governing Body is informed at the next quarterly meeting through the Administrator, and that the incident is reviewed in QAPI per QA-AE-001. | Within 2 hours of the finding. |

### 6.6 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patient refuses behavioral health screening | Assigned RN documents refusal | Document the patient's refusal, the patient's stated reason, the education provided, and the clinician's clinical observation of behavioral health status. Attempt screening at the next visit. Code the OASIS behavioral health items based on clinical observation per CMS OASIS guidance for patients who cannot or will not complete the tool. | Document at the visit; reattempt at next visit. |
| Behavioral health screening not completed at SOC | Director of Nursing identifies during supervisory review | Director of Nursing directs completion within 5 business days. Assesses reason for omission and provides corrective guidance. | Completion within 5 business days. |
| PHQ-9 positive but no physician notification documented | Director of Nursing chart audit | Director of Nursing directs the assigned RN to notify the physician and document. Reviews for pattern of non-notification. | Notification within 24 hours of identification. |
| OASIS behavioral health items inconsistent with screening tool results | Director of Nursing identifies during OASIS review | Director of Nursing directs OASIS correction per CL-OA-002. Provides documentation coaching. | Correction within 5 business days. |
| Patient with known suicidal ideation stops communicating with the agency | Assigned RN and Director of Nursing | Attempt contact by telephone and, if no response, dispatch an unscheduled home visit to conduct a welfare check. If no response at the home and safety is in question, contact 911 and the patient's emergency contact. | Telephone attempt immediately; home visit or 911 within 2 hours if no contact. |

## 7. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Behavioral health screening at SOC | Behavioral Health Screening Documentation Form (Appendix A) — all tool results with item-level responses, total scores, and clinical interpretation | Assigned RN | EHR — assessment module | At SOC; within 24 hours; retained minimum 7 years |
| OASIS behavioral health items | OASIS items coded consistently with screening results and narrative | Assigned RN | EHR — OASIS module | At each OASIS time point |
| Physician notification for positive screens | Communication note with findings, notification date/time, physician response | Assigned RN | EHR — communication notes | Within 24 hours of positive screen |
| Behavioral health plan of care integration | Behavioral health findings and response plan in the plan of care | Assigned RN | EHR — plan of care | Within 24 hours of physician notification |
| MSW referral documentation | Referral details and follow-up per CL-CP-005 | MSW / Assigned RN | EHR — referral notes | Within 48 hours of referral |
| Suicidality assessment | C-SSRS or equivalent tool results, risk classification | Assigned RN | EHR — assessment module | At the visit where suicidality is identified |
| Safety plan | Written safety plan developed with patient | Assigned RN | EHR — care plan; patient copy | At the visit where suicidality is assessed |
| Director of Nursing notification for suicidality | Notification documentation | Assigned RN | EHR — clinical notes | Within 2 hours of finding |
| Incident report for high-risk suicidality | Incident report per RM-ER-002 | Assigned RN | Incident reporting system | Within 24 hours |
| Follow-up behavioral health monitoring | Visit note documentation of behavioral health status at each visit | All clinical disciplines | EHR — visit notes | At each visit |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment — Appendix B | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PHQ-2 administered at every SOC | Chart audit | ≥98% of SOC assessments with documented PHQ-2 |
| PHQ-9 administered for all PHQ-2 positive screens | Chart audit cross-referencing PHQ-2 scores ≥3 with PHQ-9 documentation | 100% — zero missed PHQ-9 for positive PHQ-2 |
| BIMS administered at every SOC and OASIS time point | Chart audit | ≥98% |
| OASIS behavioral health items consistent with screening tool results | OASIS-to-narrative cross-reference audit | ≥95% consistency |
| Physician notification within 24 hours for all positive screens | Communication note audit | ≥95% |
| Suicidality assessed for all PHQ-9 item 9 endorsements | Chart audit | 100% |
| Behavioral health referrals documented with follow-up | Referral documentation audit | ≥95% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will verify that behavioral health screening is conducted using validated tools and that OASIS behavioral health items are accurate. They will: (a) select patients with known behavioral health diagnoses and verify that appropriate screening tools were used; (b) compare OASIS behavioral health item responses to screening tool scores documented in the clinical record; (c) verify that positive screens resulted in physician notification and plan of care integration; (d) ask clinicians to describe the PHQ-2 and BIMS administration protocol. OASIS validation auditors will specifically target behavioral health items as they directly affect PDGM payment classification.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BIMS administered incorrectly or item-level responses not documented | OASIS inaccuracy; survey deficiency | Annual BIMS administration competency validation for all RNs |
| PHQ-2 positive but PHQ-9 not administered | Missed depression diagnosis; OASIS inaccuracy | EHR workflow alert requiring PHQ-9 when PHQ-2 ≥3 |
| OASIS behavioral health items coded more positively than screening tool results support | PDGM underpayment; OASIS accuracy issue | Monthly OASIS-to-screening tool cross-reference audit |
| PHQ-9 item 9 endorsed but suicidality not formally assessed | Patient safety failure; liability exposure | Require structured suicidality assessment as mandatory workflow after PHQ-9 item 9 endorsement |
| Behavioral health findings documented but no plan of care integration | Survey deficiency; fragmented care | Require plan of care update as mandatory step following positive behavioral health screen |

## 10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All RNs shall receive competency-validated training on behavioral health screening within 14 calendar days of hire and annually thereafter, covering: PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 administration, scoring, and clinical interpretation; BIMS administration and scoring per CMS OASIS-E2 guidance; GAD-7 administration and scoring; suicidality assessment using the C-SSRS; safety plan development; behavioral health referral pathways; OASIS behavioral health item coding; and documentation standards.
10.2 BIMS administration competency shall be validated by observation — the RN must demonstrate correct administration of all three BIMS components before independently conducting OASIS assessments. This shall be assessed at hire and annually.
10.3 All clinical disciplines shall receive training on behavioral health observation and reporting responsibilities — specifically, how to identify and report behavioral health changes between RN assessment visits.
10.4 All personnel within scope shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix B) within 14 calendar days of the effective date, revision, or hire.
## 11. Version Control
11.1 This policy is maintained per EN-LC-001. Only the most current approved version is valid. 11.2 Substantive revisions require Governing Body approval. 11.3 Non-substantive revisions approved by Administrator.

# CL-SD-023 — Palliative & End-of-Life Care
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |

| Policy ID | CL-SD-023 |

| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | SD — Service Delivery |
| Classification Tier | ESSENTIAL |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |

| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the standards for palliative care delivery, advance directive discussions, goals-of-care conversations, and hospice referral coordination at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. The Medicare home health benefit is a curative benefit — it requires that patients be receiving skilled services directed toward recovery, functional improvement, or management of a condition. However, many patients receiving home health services have advanced chronic illnesses, life-limiting diagnoses, or declining functional trajectories that place them at the intersection of curative and palliative care. Palliative care is not synonymous with hospice — it is an approach to care that can and should be integrated alongside curative treatment at any stage of serious illness, focusing on relief of suffering (pain, dyspnea, nausea, anxiety, existential distress), support for the patient's and family's goals, and optimization of quality of life. The home health clinician is often the first healthcare professional to recognize that a patient's trajectory is declining, that the patient has unmet palliative care needs, or that the patient and family have not had an informed conversation about their goals and options. The clinical, ethical, and legal obligations that arise at this juncture — around advance directives, goals-of-care conversations, CPR preferences, and the transition to hospice — require that every clinician at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. has the knowledge, skill, and clear procedural guidance to navigate them with competence, compassion, and legal precision. This policy implements 42 CFR § 484.60 (plan of care conformance), CL-PR-002 (Advance Directive Compliance), and the clinical standards of the National Consensus Project for Quality Palliative Care Clinical Practice Guidelines.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All registered nurses (RNs) providing skilled nursing to patients with serious, advanced, or life-limiting illness
All licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) who may encounter patients with palliative care needs
All clinical disciplines (PT, OT, SLP, MSW) whose services intersect with palliative care goals
Medical Social Workers — the primary coordinator of psychosocial palliative care support and hospice referral
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager
All clinical disciplines who interact with patients approaching end of life
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. is committed to delivering palliative care principles — symptom management, goals-of-care alignment, psychosocial and spiritual support, and family engagement — integrated into the plan of care for every patient with a serious illness, without waiting for a prognosis of terminal illness or a decision to forgo curative treatment.
4.2 The advance directive status of every patient shall be assessed, documented, and honored as a mandatory component of the SOC assessment per CL-PR-002. Advance directive documentation shall be accessible to all treating clinicians at every visit.
4.3 The assigned RN and MSW shall engage in ongoing, sensitive, and patient-directed goals-of-care conversations throughout the episode, recognizing the patient's right to understand their prognosis, their treatment options, and the choices available to them — including the option of transitioning to hospice care.
4.4 Patients with progressive, life-limiting illnesses whose clinical trajectory suggests declining functional status or who repeatedly experience hospitalizations for the same underlying condition shall be proactively assessed for their palliative care needs, and a discussion of goals of care — including hospice eligibility — shall be initiated with the patient and caregiver in collaboration with the attending physician.
4.5 Hospice referral shall be initiated when: (a) the physician believes the patient has a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course; (b) the patient is no longer interested in curative or life-prolonging treatment; (c) the patient's clinical trajectory suggests that the goals of home health care (functional improvement, recovery) are no longer achievable; or (d) the patient and family independently request information about hospice. Hospice referral shall be coordinated per Section 6.5 and CL-CP-007 (Transfer & Referral Procedures).
4.6 Symptoms commonly associated with serious illness and end of life — including pain, dyspnea, nausea, constipation (especially opioid-induced), anxiety, agitation, oral secretions, and delirium — shall be managed with the same clinical rigor applied to any other clinical condition, using physician-ordered pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic interventions, with documented assessment, intervention, and reassessment at every applicable visit.
4.7 Spiritual and cultural needs at end of life shall be assessed and addressed as part of the plan of care. Clinicians shall not impose personal beliefs on patients or families, shall seek to understand the patient's and family's cultural and spiritual framework for illness and death, and shall coordinate chaplaincy or spiritual care resources when indicated.
4.8 Family and caregiver support during serious illness and after patient death is a recognized component of palliative care. MSW and nursing shall assess caregiver burden, grief, and bereavement needs, and shall coordinate appropriate support resources.
4.9 No patient shall be referred to hospice without their informed consent and the consent of their legal representative where applicable. The hospice election is the patient's choice — the agency's role is to ensure the patient and family have the information they need to make an informed decision.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Palliative Care | Specialized medical care focused on providing relief from the symptoms, pain, and stress of a serious illness, with the goal of improving quality of life for both the patient and family. Palliative care is appropriate at any age and at any stage in a serious illness and can be provided along with curative treatment. |
| Hospice Care | A type of palliative care for people who are nearing the end of life and have elected to forgo curative or life-prolonging treatment in favor of comfort-focused care. Under Medicare, hospice is a benefit elected by the patient when a physician certifies a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the disease runs its normal course. |
| Advance Directive | A legal document expressing a patient's wishes regarding medical treatment in the event the patient is unable to make or communicate decisions. Common forms include a Living Will and a Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare (DPAHC). |
| POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) | A portable, physician-signed medical order that translates a patient's goals and preferences for life-sustaining treatment into immediately actionable physician orders — including CPR preferences, level of medical intervention, and artificial nutrition. In California, this form is called the POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment). |
| Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) | A physician's order directing that cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) shall not be attempted in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest. |
| Goals-of-Care Conversation | A structured, compassionate dialogue between the clinical team and the patient and/or family to understand the patient's values, priorities, and preferences for medical treatment, and to align the plan of care with those goals. |
| Prognosis | The physician's assessment of the likely course and outcome of the patient's illness. |
| Life-Limiting Illness | An illness that is expected to shorten the patient's life, including advanced cancer, advanced heart failure (NYHA Class III–IV), advanced COPD (GOLD Stage III–IV), end-stage renal disease, advanced dementia, advanced liver disease, and ALS. |
| Bereavement | The experience of grief following the death of a loved one. |
| Caregiver Burnout | A state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion that can occur when caregivers don't get the help they need or try to do more than they are able — physically or financially. |
| Dyspnea | Subjective experience of breathing discomfort that consists of qualitatively distinct sensations that vary in intensity — particularly distressing in end-of-life care and requiring aggressive symptom management. |
| Delirium | An acute onset neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by fluctuating disturbances in attention, awareness, and cognition — common in the final days and weeks of life and requiring careful symptom assessment and management. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Advance Directive Assessment at SOC

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned RN | At the SOC visit, assess the patient's advance directive status as a mandatory component of the comprehensive assessment. Ask: "Do you have any documents that express your wishes about medical care if you were unable to make decisions for yourself — such as a Living Will or a Healthcare Power of Attorney?" Document the patient's response. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned RN | If the patient has an advance directive: (a) request a copy or verify that a copy is in the clinical record; (b) document the type of advance directive (Living Will, DPAHC, POLST, DNR order, or combination); (c) review the contents with the patient to verify that the document reflects their current wishes; (d) document the name and contact information of the designated healthcare agent (DPAHC); (e) place a copy in the patient's clinical record and note its accessibility in the plan of care; (f) ensure all treating clinicians are informed of the advance directive status. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned RN | If the patient does not have an advance directive: (a) provide information about advance directives per CL-PR-002 — what they are, why they are beneficial, how to create them; (b) provide written educational materials in the patient's primary language per OP-PA-003; (c) document that information was provided and the patient's response; (d) offer to facilitate the process and refer to the MSW if the patient is interested in assistance. Do not pressure the patient to create an advance directive. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.4 | Assigned RN | For patients with a DNR or POLST in place: verify the document is current, properly signed by the physician, and accessible in the home in a location the patient and caregiver can immediately retrieve in an emergency. In California, the POLST shall be signed by a physician and maintained in a location where emergency responders can find it — typically on the refrigerator door. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.5 | Assigned RN | Assess and document the OASIS advance care planning item (M1051 — "Has a formal legal document been completed to express the patient's wishes regarding life-sustaining treatment?") accurately and consistently with the clinical record per CL-OA-007. | At the SOC visit within 24 hours. |

### 6.2 Ongoing Palliative Care Assessment and Integration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN | At each visit for patients with life-limiting or serious illness, assess the following palliative care domains: (a) Symptom burden — pain (per CL-SD-014), dyspnea, nausea, constipation, fatigue, oral secretions, delirium (if in the final phase); (b) Functional trajectory — is the patient's functional status improving, stable, or declining compared to the prior visit and to admission? (c) Goals alignment — are the current treatments and goals of care aligned with what the patient has expressed as most important to them? (d) Caregiver burden — how is the caregiver coping? What is their understanding of the patient's prognosis? (e) Spiritual and existential needs — is the patient or family expressing existential distress, fear, unfinished business, or spiritual needs that are unaddressed? | At each visit. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN | Document the palliative care assessment in the visit note with sufficient specificity to demonstrate active clinical engagement with the patient's quality of life and symptom burden — not merely "patient is stable" or "patient is comfortable." | Within 24 hours of each visit. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN | When the patient's clinical trajectory suggests a transition is approaching (declining functional status, increasing symptom burden, multiple hospitalizations for the same underlying condition, weight loss >10% of body weight in 6 months), document the observation, notify the Director of Nursing, and initiate a goals-of-care conversation process per Section 6.3. | Within 24 hours of identifying a trajectory change. |

### 6.3 Goals-of-Care Conversations

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN / MSW | When a goals-of-care conversation is indicated, coordinate the conversation to involve the assigned RN, the MSW (if involved), and — where possible — the attending physician. Identify the most appropriate setting (the patient's home, a family meeting if multiple family members are involved) and the appropriate timing (when the patient is comfortable, rested, and not in acute distress). | Before the conversation; scheduled within 48 hours of identifying the need. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN / MSW | Conduct the goals-of-care conversation using evidence-based communication frameworks (REMAP, SPIKES, or equivalent): (a) Ask what the patient and family understand about the current illness and prognosis; (b) Listen to understand the patient's values, fears, and hopes; (c) Inform the patient about the current clinical situation, prognosis, and treatment options in plain, compassionate language — avoid medical jargon; (d) Acknowledge the patient's emotional response — normalize grief, fear, and uncertainty; (e) Explore the patient's goals — what matters most to them? What are they hoping for? What are they afraid of? (f) Align recommendations with the patient's expressed goals. | At the goals-of-care conversation. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN / MSW | Document the goals-of-care conversation in the clinical record, including: (a) the participants; (b) the patient's and family's expressed understanding of the prognosis; (c) the patient's stated values and goals (what matters most); (d) any treatment preferences expressed (CPR, hospitalization, artificial nutrition, aggressive intervention); (e) any referrals or consultations discussed; (f) the plan going forward as agreed upon by the patient, family, and clinical team; (g) the physician's involvement or the plan to involve the physician. | Within 24 hours of the conversation. |
| 6.3.4 | Assigned RN | If the goals-of-care conversation reveals that the patient's goals are inconsistent with the current treatment plan (e.g., patient does not want further hospitalization but has no DNR, patient wants to focus on comfort but is on curative chemotherapy), notify the physician within 24 hours to facilitate plan revision. | Within 24 hours. |

### 6.4 Symptom Management at End of Life

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assigned RN | Assess and manage the following common end-of-life symptoms at each visit, using physician-ordered interventions: (a) Pain — per CL-SD-014; for patients transitioning to comfort care, pain management shall be prioritized over concerns about opioid adverse effects; titration to comfort is the goal. (b) Dyspnea — assess using the Modified Borg Dyspnea Scale or numeric rating; manage with physician-ordered opioids (opioids are the most effective pharmacologic treatment for dyspnea at end of life and shall not be withheld out of respiratory depression concern in patients who are comfort-focused); supplemental oxygen if beneficial; positioning (head of bed elevated, fan directed toward face); pursed-lip breathing if tolerated. (c) Nausea and vomiting — assess frequency and triggers; administer antiemetics per physician order; address reversible causes (constipation, medications). (d) Constipation — a universal side effect of opioid therapy; assess bowel function at every visit; ensure a bowel regimen is in place for all patients on opioids; contact physician if no bowel movement in >3 days. (e) Agitation and delirium — assess using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) or clinical observation; identify and manage reversible causes (urinary retention, constipation, pain, medications); administer physician-ordered antipsychotics or benzodiazepines for terminal agitation; maintain a calm, quiet environment; keep family informed. (f) Oral secretions (death rattle) — position the patient laterally; administer physician-ordered anticholinergic medications; educate family that the sound is not distressing to the patient. (g) Mouth care — provide or teach aggressive mouth care (every 2 hours) for patients with dry mouth or who are not eating or drinking. | At each visit for patients in the palliative/end-of-life phase. |
| 6.4.2 | Assigned RN | Document each symptom assessment with a validated score or objective observation, the intervention provided, and the patient's response following the intervention. | Within 24 hours of each visit. |
| 6.4.3 | Assigned RN | Contact the physician within 4 hours when any end-of-life symptom is not controlled by the current medication regimen, to obtain orders for dose adjustment, additional medications, or alternative interventions. | Within 4 hours of identifying uncontrolled symptoms. |

### 6.5 Hospice Referral Coordination

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Assigned RN / MSW | When hospice referral is clinically indicated or patient-requested, initiate the hospice conversation as a collaborative process: (a) Ensure the patient and family understand what hospice is — a Medicare-covered benefit providing comfort-focused care at home, including 24-hour nursing support, medications for the terminal diagnosis, durable medical equipment, social work, chaplaincy, and bereavement support; (b) Ensure the patient and family understand what hospice is not — it is not giving up, it is not hastening death, and the patient may revoke hospice at any time; (c) Ensure the patient and family understand that electing hospice means changing the focus from curative to comfort care, which typically involves stopping curative treatments for the terminal diagnosis; (d) Answer questions honestly and compassionately, using plain language. | When clinically indicated or patient-requested. |
| 6.5.2 | Assigned RN | Notify the attending physician that hospice referral is being considered, provide a clinical summary of the patient's trajectory, and request the physician's input and, if appropriate, certification of a terminal prognosis of 6 months or less. | Within 24 hours of the hospice conversation initiation. |
| 6.5.3 | MSW | Identify hospice agencies that serve the patient's geographic area and accept the patient's payer source (Medicare, Medi-Cal, or commercial insurance). Present options to the patient and family, respecting their right to select the hospice provider of their choice. Facilitate the referral per CL-CP-007, Section 6.4. | Within 48 hours of the patient's decision to pursue hospice. |
| 6.5.4 | Assigned RN | Coordinate the clinical transition: (a) prepare the clinical transfer summary per CL-CP-007 Appendix A; (b) conduct a warm handoff with the hospice admitting nurse; (c) transmit the complete medication list, advance directive documentation, and relevant clinical records to the hospice agency; (d) complete the discharge OASIS for the home health episode. | Before or on the date of hospice election. |
| 6.5.5 | Assigned RN | Ensure that the patient and family have been informed that: (a) home health and hospice cannot be provided simultaneously for the same terminal diagnosis under Medicare (the patient must elect one or the other); (b) the patient may revoke hospice at any time; (c) the agency's staff will remain available for questions until the hospice agency assumes care. | At the time of the transition discussion. |

### 6.6 Bereavement Support

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.6.1 | MSW / Assigned RN | When a patient who is receiving home health services dies at home (not transferred to hospice), the assigned RN or on-call nurse shall respond to the family's contact, assess the situation, provide emotional support to the family, and ensure the appropriate notification procedures are followed (physician notification, coroner if applicable per California law). | Immediately upon notification. |
| 6.6.2 | MSW | When the agency becomes aware of a patient's death (whether the patient was receiving home health at the time of death or had been recently discharged), the MSW shall contact the family within 5 business days to offer condolences and assess bereavement needs. Provide information about grief support resources in the community. | Within 5 business days of learning of the death. |
| 6.6.3 | Director of Nursing | Document all staff responses to patient deaths, including nursing response, MSW bereavement contact, and any referrals made for family bereavement support. | Within 5 business days. |

### 6.7 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patient or family expresses a desire to transition to comfort care but physician is not engaging with the conversation | Director of Nursing and MSW escalate to Administrator | Administrator contacts the physician or physician practice administration in writing to communicate the patient's expressed goals and request a goals-of-care conversation. If the situation remains unresolved, consult the Compliance Officer and Legal Counsel. | Director of Nursing contact within 48 hours; Administrator within 7 calendar days. |
| Patient has an advance directive but clinical team is unsure whether to honor it in a specific situation | Director of Nursing consults with Administrator and Legal Counsel | Follow the advance directive per California law (PROBATE Code § 4600–4805). If there is genuine legal ambiguity, contact Legal Counsel. Do not override an advance directive without legal or physician guidance. | Legal consult initiated within 24 hours. |
| Patient's legally designated surrogate decision-maker and the clinical team disagree about the plan of care | Director of Nursing, Administrator, and Compliance Officer | Facilitate a family meeting. Involve the attending physician. Document all communications. If the disagreement cannot be resolved clinically, contact Legal Counsel. | Family meeting within 48 hours. |
| Uncontrolled end-of-life symptoms not responsive to current physician orders | Assigned RN notifies physician immediately | Physician adjusts orders urgently. If the patient is in severe distress and the physician is unreachable, activate the on-call protocol per OP-SL-002 and document all actions. | Physician contact immediately; on-call activation if unreachable. |
| Clinician is uncomfortable participating in a goals-of-care or hospice discussion | Clinician notifies Director of Nursing | Director of Nursing assigns a more experienced clinician to lead the conversation. Provides training and support to the uncomfortable clinician without repercussion. | Reassignment within 24 hours. |

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |

| Advance directive assessment at SOC | Type, content, location, and DPAHC designation | Assigned RN | EHR — assessment module | At SOC; within 24 hours; retained minimum 7 years |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advance directive status assessed and documented at SOC | Chart audit | ≥98% of SOC records with advance directive assessment |
| OASIS advance care planning item consistent with clinical documentation | OASIS-to-narrative cross-reference audit | ≥95% consistency |
| Goals-of-care conversations documented for patients with life-limiting illness | Chart audit of palliative care patients | ≥95% with documented conversation when clinically indicated |
| End-of-life symptom assessments include validated scores and documented interventions | Chart audit | ≥90% of palliative care visits with validated symptom scores |
| Hospice referral coordination complete with warm handoff documentation | Referral documentation audit | ≥95% of hospice transitions with documented warm handoff |
| Bereavement contact made within 5 business days of patient death | MSW documentation audit | ≥90% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will verify that advance directives are assessed, documented, and accessible in the clinical record. They will ask clinical staff whether they know how to access the advance directive for any patient they are caring for. Surveyors will also examine whether the plan of care reflects the patient's expressed goals — a plan of care focused on aggressive functional restoration for a patient who has expressed comfort-only goals is an alignment failure. ADR auditors will examine whether palliative care visits are documented with sufficient clinical specificity to support skilled nursing — a visit note that reads "patient comfortable" without symptom assessment or documented interventions does not demonstrate skilled care.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advance directive assessed but document not in the clinical record | Directive not accessible in an emergency; survey deficiency | Require copy of advance directive in the EHR before the second visit |
| POLST not accessible in the home where emergency responders can find it | Emergency responders may perform unwanted CPR | Provide POLST placement education at SOC — refrigerator door is the California standard |
| Goals-of-care conversations occurring but not documented | No evidence of patient-centered care; plan of care misalignment | Require documentation within 24 hours; EHR care coordination note template |
| Dyspnea managed solely with oxygen without opioid consideration in comfort-focused patients | Uncontrolled suffering; inadequate end-of-life care | Train all RNs on opioid use for dyspnea in comfort-focused care; physician communication protocol |
| Hospice transition not coordinated — patient discharged without warm handoff | Fragmented care; patient and family abandoned at the most vulnerable moment | CL-CP-007 hospice transfer protocol mandatory; Director of Nursing reviews all hospice transitions |

## 10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All RNs and MSWs shall receive competency-validated training on palliative and end-of-life care within 14 calendar days of hire and annually thereafter, covering: palliative care principles and the distinction between palliative care and hospice; advance directive types, legal requirements under California law, and POLST execution; goals-of-care communication skills using an evidence-based framework (REMAP, SPIKES, or equivalent); end-of-life symptom assessment and management (pain, dyspnea, delirium, constipation, secretions); opioid use for dyspnea in comfort-focused patients; hospice referral coordination per CL-CP-007; bereavement support; and documentation standards for palliative care visits demonstrating skilled nursing.
10.2 All clinical disciplines shall receive training on advance directive status awareness — they must be able to identify whether a patient has an advance directive and know where to find it in the clinical record.
10.3 All personnel within scope shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix B) within 14 calendar days of the effective date, revision, or hire.

# CL-SD-024 — Missed Visit & Rescheduling
## 1. Policy Header

| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the protocols for managing, documenting, and reporting missed visits and rescheduling requirements at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. A missed visit is any scheduled patient visit that does not occur as planned — regardless of whether it was missed due to patient refusal, patient unavailability, clinician absence, scheduling error, or emergency. Missed visits are significant clinical events: they represent a gap in skilled care delivery, potentially interrupt therapeutic treatment sequences, increase the risk of clinical deterioration going undetected, and — when not properly documented and managed — create documentation integrity failures, LUPA risk, and False Claims Act exposure if the ordered visit frequency is not delivered but a full episode payment is collected. The CMS Home Health Compare quality measure "Timely Initiation of Care" and the PDGM LUPA threshold both create direct financial and quality consequences for visits that are not delivered as ordered. This policy ensures that every missed visit is identified on the same day it occurs, is documented with the reason and the clinical assessment of patient impact, is rescheduled within the shortest clinically appropriate timeframe, is communicated to the physician when clinically significant, and is tracked through the QAPI program as a quality indicator.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All clinical disciplines (RN, LVN, PT, OT, SLP, MSW, HHA) who experience or identify missed patient visits
Clinical Coordinators responsible for managing visit scheduling and rescheduling
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager responsible for clinical oversight and missed visit response
Revenue Cycle staff monitoring LUPA risk and visit frequency compliance
The QAPI Coordinator tracking missed visit rates as a quality indicator
This policy applies to all types of missed visits for all disciplines during any phase of the home health episode.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Every missed visit shall be identified on the day it was scheduled and shall be documented in the patient's clinical record on the same day with: (a) the type of visit missed (discipline, visit number in the episode); (b) the reason for the missed visit; (c) the responsible party for the missed visit (patient, caregiver, clinician, scheduling error, emergency, weather, other); (d) the clinical assessment of patient impact — what clinical risk does the missed visit create for this specific patient?; (e) the rescheduling plan.
4.2 Every missed visit shall be rescheduled at the earliest clinically appropriate opportunity. Rescheduling does not mean adding a visit to the end of the certification period — it means providing the missed visit as soon as the patient is available and clinically appropriate to do so. The goal is minimal disruption to the patient's therapeutic trajectory.
4.3 The reason for every missed visit shall be classified using the agency's standard missed visit reason taxonomy (Appendix A) to enable accurate QAPI tracking and identification of systemic causes.
4.4 The physician shall be notified within 24 hours of a missed visit when: (a) the patient refused care and the refusal creates a patient safety concern; (b) the missed visit disrupts a critical clinical sequence (e.g., missed wound care, missed insulin administration, missed critical medication monitoring); (c) more than 2 consecutive visits in any discipline have been missed; (d) the patient was not available at home and was not reachable by telephone — raising a potential welfare concern.
4.5 If a patient cannot be reached by telephone and was not found at home for a scheduled visit, the clinical coordinator or assigned clinician shall attempt contact using all known telephone numbers and emergency contacts within 4 hours of the missed visit. If the patient is still unreachable after 4 hours, notify the Director of Nursing immediately. The Director of Nursing shall assess whether a welfare check is warranted and shall coordinate with the physician and, if necessary, emergency services.
4.6 Patient refusal of a visit shall be documented with specificity: the refusal shall be documented in the patient's clinical record with the patient's specific stated reason (not "patient refused"), any education or counseling provided regarding the clinical implications of the refusal, and the plan for the next visit.
4.7 Repeated missed visits — defined as 3 or more missed visits in any discipline within a 30-day period for the same patient — shall trigger a clinical case review by the Director of Nursing to assess: the patient's engagement and adherence barriers; whether the plan of care is appropriate and achievable; whether non-compliance discharge criteria per CL-CP-006 Section 6.5 may be applicable; and what interventions can improve care delivery.
4.8 All missed visits shall be tracked in the agency's QAPI dashboard per QA-PI-002 as a quality indicator. The Director of Nursing shall report missed visit rates, reasons, and trends to the QAPI Committee quarterly. A missed visit rate exceeding agency-defined threshold shall trigger a Performance Improvement Project per QA-PI-001.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Missed Visit | Any scheduled patient visit in any clinical discipline that did not occur as planned, for any reason. |
| Patient Refusal | A missed visit in which the patient or legal representative declined the visit at the scheduled time or in advance, with sufficient notice that the visit was not attempted or was attempted and declined at the door. |
| Clinician Unavailability | A missed visit caused by the assigned clinician's absence due to illness, emergency, scheduling conflict, or other clinician-side reason. |
| Patient Unavailability | A missed visit in which the patient was not at home at the scheduled visit time without prior notification, was not responsive to door knocking or calling, or was present but physically unable to participate in the visit due to acute illness requiring emergency transport. |
| Scheduling Error | A missed visit caused by an administrative failure — incorrect visit date or time communicated to the patient or clinician, scheduling system error, or failure to schedule a visit that was ordered. |
| LUPA Risk | The risk that a patient's episode will have fewer visits than the CMS-defined minimum visit threshold for their PDGM payment category, resulting in a Low Utilization Payment Adjustment (reduced payment). |
| Welfare Check | A safety assessment initiated when a patient is unreachable and there is concern for their safety, typically conducted by the agency (unscheduled home visit) or emergency services (911). |
| Therapeutic Trajectory | The planned sequence of clinical interventions and the anticipated functional or clinical progress expected from that sequence over the course of the episode. |
| Consecutive Missed Visits | Two or more visits in the same discipline, ordered on consecutive visit days or within a defined short interval, that were both missed without delivery. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Same-Day Identification and Documentation

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned Clinician / Clinical Coordinator | On the day of any scheduled visit that does not occur, document a Missed Visit Record in the patient's EHR within 4 hours of the scheduled visit time. The Missed Visit Record shall include all fields specified in Section 4.1. | Within 4 hours of the scheduled visit time. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned Clinician / Clinical Coordinator | Classify the reason for the missed visit using the Missed Visit Reason Taxonomy (Appendix A). Select the most accurate reason code and add a narrative description if needed. | At the time of Missed Visit Record completion. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned Clinician | Document the clinical assessment of patient impact: (a) What specific clinical activities were planned for this visit that did not occur? (b) What is the clinical risk of a one-visit gap for this specific patient (considering their diagnoses, current treatment phase, and stability)? (c) Is there an immediate clinical safety concern resulting from this missed visit? | At the time of Missed Visit Record completion. |
| 6.1.4 | Clinical Coordinator | Update the visit scheduling system to reflect the missed visit and the rescheduling action taken, ensuring accurate visit delivery tracking for LUPA monitoring. | Within 4 hours of the scheduled visit time. |

### 6.2 Rescheduling Protocol

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Clinical Coordinator | Contact the patient or caregiver to reschedule the missed visit at the earliest clinically appropriate opportunity. The rescheduling target is: (a) For critical clinical visits (wound care, medication administration, post-hospitalization ROC, insulin management, cardiac monitoring) — reschedule within 24 hours; (b) For standard skilled visits — reschedule within 48 hours; (c) For supplementary visits (education-only, non-critical monitoring) — reschedule within 72 hours. | Per the schedule above. |
| 6.2.2 | Clinical Coordinator | Document the rescheduling action in the Missed Visit Record: the date and time of the rescheduled visit, the method of patient contact, and the patient's confirmation. | At the time of rescheduling. |
| 6.2.3 | Director of Nursing | For missed visits classified as high clinical impact (wound care, post-operative care, medication-dependent visits, post-hospitalization visits), the Director of Nursing shall verify that rescheduling occurs within 24 hours and shall review the missed visit documentation for adequacy. | Within 24 hours of the high-impact missed visit. |
| 6.2.4 | Clinical Coordinator | Monitor the LUPA risk status for all active episodes following any missed visit. If a missed visit creates or increases LUPA risk for an episode, notify the Director of Nursing immediately for clinical review per QA-PI-006 and CL-SD-025. | On the same day as the missed visit documentation. |

### 6.3 Patient Not Found / Welfare Check Protocol

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Visiting Clinician | If the patient is not at home at the scheduled visit time, the clinician shall: (a) attempt to reach the patient by telephone using all numbers in the clinical record; (b) if reachable — document the reason, reschedule per Section 6.2, and complete the Missed Visit Record; (c) if not reachable at the home — contact the Clinical Coordinator immediately. | Immediately upon discovering the patient is not home. |
| 6.3.2 | Clinical Coordinator | Attempt to reach the patient and all emergency contacts using all available telephone numbers. Document every contact attempt with the date, time, method, and result. | Within 2 hours of the clinician's report. |
| 6.3.3 | Director of Nursing | If the patient cannot be reached after all contact attempts by 4 hours post-scheduled visit time, the Director of Nursing shall assess the patient's risk level: (a) Low risk — patient is known to be active, mobile, and has a reliable caregiver; continue contact attempts and schedule a welfare check visit for the next day; (b) Moderate risk — patient lives alone, has cognitive impairment, or has a recent hospitalization; dispatch an unscheduled welfare check visit on the same day; (c) High risk — patient has advanced illness, lives alone, has a history of falls, or has not been reached for more than 8 hours; call 911 to request a welfare check. | Assessment within 4 hours; 911 for high-risk patients. |
| 6.3.4 | Director of Nursing | Document all welfare check actions in the patient's clinical record, including every contact attempt, the risk assessment, the actions taken, and the outcome. | Within 24 hours of the resolution. |
| 6.3.5 | Assigned RN | Notify the physician within 24 hours of any patient not-found event, regardless of ultimate outcome, documenting the notification and the physician's response. | Within 24 hours. |

### 6.4 Patient Refusal Documentation

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Visiting Clinician | When a patient refuses a scheduled visit, document the refusal in the Missed Visit Record and in the visit note with specificity: (a) the patient's specific stated reason for refusal (not "patient refused" — document the actual reason given); (b) the clinician's assessment of whether the refusal reflects a cognitive or capacity issue versus an informed choice; (c) the education or counseling provided regarding the clinical implications of not receiving the visit; (d) any patient safety concern identified as a result of the refusal; (e) the rescheduling plan or the plan to address the refusal at the next visit. | Within 4 hours of the refusal. |
| 6.4.2 | Visiting Clinician | If the patient's refusal creates an immediate patient safety concern (patient is refusing wound care on an infected wound, patient is refusing insulin management and is known to have poorly controlled blood glucose), notify the assigned RN and Director of Nursing within 2 hours. The RN shall notify the physician within 24 hours. | Within 2 hours of a safety-significant refusal. |
| 6.4.3 | Assigned RN | If a patient repeatedly refuses visits in the same discipline (3 or more refusals within 30 days), assess: (a) whether the refusals reflect a pattern of informed patient choice (the patient does not find the service beneficial or is uncomfortable with a particular clinician); (b) whether the refusals reflect a capacity concern; (c) whether the plan of care is appropriate for this patient; and initiate the clinical case review per Section 4.7. | Assessment within 7 calendar days of the third refusal. |

### 6.5 Repeated Missed Visit Clinical Case Review

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Director of Nursing | When triggered by 3 or more missed visits in any discipline within 30 days for the same patient, conduct a clinical case review within 7 calendar days, assessing: (a) the pattern of missed visits — same time of day, same day of week, same discipline, patient-initiated vs. agency-initiated; (b) the patient's engagement level and stated barriers; (c) the clinical necessity of the current visit frequency — is it ordered at the right frequency for the patient's current status? (d) the adequacy of the caregiver's ability to support visit delivery; (e) whether MSW involvement is needed to address barriers; (f) whether the plan of care requires modification per CL-CP-002; (g) whether non-compliance discharge considerations apply per CL-CP-006 Section 6.5. | Within 7 calendar days of the triggering third missed visit. |
| 6.5.2 | Director of Nursing | Document the case review findings and the action plan, including: any plan of care modifications; any scheduling changes; any MSW referral; any counseling provided to the patient; and the physician notification. | Within 7 calendar days of the review. |
| 6.5.3 | Director of Nursing | Notify the physician of the missed visit pattern and the case review findings within 24 hours of completing the review. | Within 24 hours of review completion. |

### 6.6 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Clinician missed the visit due to scheduling error | Clinical Coordinator and Director of Nursing | Reschedule immediately. Assess whether the scheduling error was systemic. Director of Nursing provides corrective guidance to scheduling staff. | Rescheduling within 24 hours; root cause assessment within 5 business days. |
| Patient not found and cannot be reached — high risk | Director of Nursing calls 911 | Emergency welfare check. Physician notification. Incident report per RM-ER-002 if patient is found to have experienced a clinical emergency. | 911 immediately for high-risk; incident report within 24 hours. |
| Missed visits are creating LUPA risk | Revenue Cycle and Director of Nursing | Per QA-PI-006 and CL-SD-025 — clinical review, scheduling adjustment, physician contact if additional visits are warranted. | Immediate review; action within 24 hours. |
| Clinician documents a missed visit more than 24 hours after the scheduled visit | Director of Nursing chart review | Director of Nursing provides corrective guidance. Clinician completes a late-entry notation per CO-DC-003. | Documentation completed within 24 hours of identification. |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All missed visits documented within 4 hours | EHR timestamp audit | ≥95% of missed visits documented within 4 hours |
| All missed visits rescheduled within the category-appropriate timeframe | Rescheduling date audit vs. missed visit date | ≥90% rescheduled within the target timeframe |
| Physician notified within 24 hours for all notification-trigger missed visits | Communication note audit | ≥95% |
| Welfare check protocol activated for all not-found high-risk patients | Director of Nursing documentation audit | 100% |
| Monthly missed visit rate tracked in QAPI dashboard | QAPI dashboard review | Rate tracked and reported; threshold-triggered PIP initiated |
| Repeated missed visit case reviews completed within 7 calendar days | Case review documentation audit | ≥95% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will verify that missed visits are documented as such — they will review visit schedules and identify any ordered visits for which no visit note exists, and they will check whether a Missed Visit Record was completed. Surveyors will also verify that patient refusals are documented with specific reasons rather than the generic notation "patient refused." ADR auditors will cross-reference ordered visit frequency against delivered visit documentation — undelivered ordered visits that appear as billable in claims are False Claims Act risk items.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missed visit not documented — clinician simply doesn't complete a note | Documentation gap; survey citation; inability to demonstrate compliance with ordered frequency | EHR alert for scheduled visits with no corresponding visit note or missed visit record by end of day |
| Patient refusal documented as "pt refused" without specific reason | Survey deficiency; inadequate documentation | Require specific refusal reason field in the missed visit record |
| Not-found patient not followed up for welfare check | Patient safety failure; liability | Director of Nursing notification protocol automatically triggered at 4 hours of no patient contact |
| LUPA risk from missed visits not identified until claim submission | Revenue loss; billing compliance issue | Daily LUPA risk monitoring integrated into the scheduling system |
