10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All agency personnel who have direct patient contact shall receive training on the restraint prohibition within 14 calendar days of hire and annually thereafter, including: the absolute prohibition on physical and chemical restraints; the definition of a chemical restraint distinguished from a therapeutic medication; the protocol for managing unsafe patient behavior without restraint; de-escalation techniques; the response when caregiver restraint use is discovered; and the mandatory reporting obligation.
10.2 Scenario-based training using realistic home health clinical situations shall be incorporated into annual restraint training to ensure that clinicians can apply the policy in practice — not just recall its provisions.
10.3 All personnel within scope shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix A) within 14 calendar days of the effective date, any revision, or hire/appointment.
11. Version Control
11.1 Maintained per EN-LC-001. Only the most current approved version is valid. 11.2 Substantive revisions require Governing Body approval, re-acknowledgment within 14 calendar days, and policy index update per EN-TG-001. 11.3 Non-substantive revisions approved by Administrator with Governing Body notification.

## CL-PR-005 — Emergency Preparedness — Clinical
### 1. Policy Header

### 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the clinical protocols, patient-facing emergency communication standards, clinical continuity requirements, and individual patient emergency planning obligations that Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. maintains to protect every patient during emergencies and disasters. Emergency preparedness in home health is not simply a plan that lives in a binder — it is an operational clinical responsibility that activates the moment a disaster is declared, a patient is stranded without caregiver support, a power outage threatens a patient who is technology-dependent, or an infectious disease outbreak disrupts the agency's ability to deliver scheduled visits.
The home health patient population is among the most vulnerable in any emergency: homebound, often without immediate social support, frequently dependent on electricity-powered medical equipment, managing complex medication regimens that require refrigeration or precise timing, and unable to self-evacuate. When a hurricane approaches, when wildfires force evacuations, when a prolonged power outage occurs, or when a pandemic disrupts the workforce — the agency's clinical team is often the only professional lifeline between the patient and a preventable clinical catastrophe.
Federal law requires that Medicare-certified home health agencies maintain an emergency preparedness program under 42 CFR § 484.102. This Condition of Participation requires: a risk assessment-based emergency plan; policies and procedures implementing that plan; a communication plan; and a training and testing program. This policy governs the clinical dimensions of that requirement — specifically, the protocols governing how the agency identifies which patients are most vulnerable in emergencies, communicates with patients during and after a declared emergency, ensures continuity of clinical care for at-risk patients, manages technology-dependent patients, coordinates with community emergency management systems, and documents all emergency-period clinical activities. The agency's operational Emergency Operations and Business Continuity Plan is established in policy OP-FM-005. This policy is the clinical implementation arm of that broader plan.
### 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All registered nurses and licensed vocational nurses responsible for assigned patient caseloads
All clinical disciplines (PT, OT, SLP, MSW, HHA) whose patients may be affected by emergencies
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager who directs clinical emergency response
The Administrator who activates the Emergency Operations Plan
Clinical Coordinators who manage patient communication and visit scheduling during emergencies
On-call nursing staff who may be the first clinical point of contact during an emergency event
All contracted clinical staff providing services under agency authorization
This policy applies during all declared emergencies — whether declared by federal, state, or local government — and during any event that significantly disrupts the agency's ability to deliver scheduled clinical services, regardless of whether a formal declaration has been issued. It applies to every patient on the active census at the time of the emergency.
### 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. shall maintain a continuously updated Patient Emergency Risk Stratification System that classifies every active patient by their level of vulnerability during an emergency, enabling the agency to triage its limited clinical resources to the patients with the greatest clinical need when emergency conditions limit the agency's capacity to serve all patients simultaneously.
4.2 The agency shall maintain current emergency contact information — including at least two emergency contacts beyond the primary caregiver — for every active patient in the clinical record, updated at each visit and verified at each OASIS time point.
4.3 The agency shall develop and maintain an individualized Emergency Preparedness Care Plan (EPCP) for every patient identified as High Risk (Category 1) under the Patient Emergency Risk Stratification System. The EPCP shall be incorporated into the patient's plan of care and shall identify: the specific emergency risks to the patient; the patient's emergency shelter option; the patient's backup caregiver arrangements; the management plan for technology dependence; medication contingency planning; and the patient's designated emergency representative contact.
4.4 During any declared emergency or significant service disruption, the Director of Nursing shall activate the Clinical Emergency Response Protocol, which establishes priority contact sequences, alternative visit delivery mechanisms, and clinical triage decision-making frameworks for managing patient care during the emergency period.
4.5 The agency shall ensure that every technology-dependent patient — including patients using electrically powered medical equipment such as home ventilators, oxygen concentrators, infusion pumps, home dialysis equipment, or feeding pumps — has an individualized technology failure contingency plan documented in the plan of care and in the patient's EPCP.
4.6 The agency shall communicate with all active patients within 24 hours of the onset of any emergency event that disrupts normal service delivery, assess patient safety and clinical status, and document the outcome of every contact attempt.
4.7 The Director of Nursing shall prioritize clinical resources during emergencies based on the Patient Emergency Risk Stratification System, ensuring that Category 1 (Highest Risk) patients receive clinical contact within 12 hours and Category 2 (High Risk) patients receive contact within 24 hours of the emergency onset.
4.8 During an emergency period, the agency shall maintain detailed documentation of: all patient contact attempts and outcomes; clinical decisions made under emergency conditions; any modifications to ordered visit frequency necessitated by the emergency; any patient adverse events that occur during the emergency period; and all coordination with community emergency management agencies, utility companies, and healthcare facilities.
4.9 The agency shall cooperate and coordinate with the local and state emergency management agency, county public health department, and Healthcare Coalition during any declared public health emergency, and shall fulfill reporting obligations under applicable state emergency protocols.
4.10 The agency shall conduct a post-emergency After-Action Review within 30 calendar days of the resolution of any declared emergency, documenting: what worked, what failed, patient adverse events attributable to the emergency, and corrective actions to improve the emergency response for future events. After-Action Review findings shall be reported to the QAPI Committee and to the Governing Body.
### 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Declared Emergency | A formal declaration of emergency by a federal, state, county, or municipal government authority that activates emergency response protocols and may trigger regulatory flexibilities for Medicare-certified providers. |
| Emergency Operations Plan (EOP) | The agency's comprehensive emergency preparedness plan established under 42 CFR § 484.102 and detailed in policy OP-FM-005, addressing all-hazards emergency response across the agency's operations. |
| Emergency Preparedness Care Plan (EPCP) | An individualized patient-level plan, incorporated into the plan of care, that identifies the patient's specific emergency vulnerabilities and establishes contingency plans for each identified risk. |
| Patient Emergency Risk Stratification | The process of classifying every active patient into a risk category based on their vulnerability during an emergency — considering technology dependence, social isolation, medication criticality, mobility limitations, and clinical complexity. |
| Category 1 — Highest Risk | Patients who are technology-dependent (ventilator, IV therapy, enteral nutrition, home dialysis), have no caregiver available during the emergency, or whose clinical condition would deteriorate rapidly without daily skilled intervention. These patients require clinical contact within 12 hours of emergency onset. |
| Category 2 — High Risk | Patients who are medically complex, receiving skilled services for unstable conditions, or whose caregivers have limited emergency coping capacity, but who are not technology-dependent. These patients require clinical contact within 24 hours. |
| Category 3 — Moderate Risk | Patients who are clinically stable, have adequate caregiver support, and can safely tolerate a brief delay in services without adverse clinical consequence. These patients require contact within 48 hours. |
| Category 4 — Lower Risk | Patients who are nearing discharge criteria, are clinically stable with highly supportive caregivers, and can safely manage independently for up to 72 hours. These patients require contact within 72 hours. |
| Technology-Dependent Patient | A patient whose clinical safety depends on the continuous or regular operation of electrically powered or battery-powered medical equipment — including but not limited to: mechanical ventilators; home oxygen concentrators; infusion pumps for IV medications; enteral feeding pumps; suction machines; and home dialysis equipment. |
| After-Action Review | A structured post-event evaluation conducted within 30 calendar days of an emergency resolution that assesses the effectiveness of the agency's emergency response, identifies gaps and failures, and establishes corrective actions. |
| Healthcare Coalition | A regional collaborative of healthcare facilities, public health agencies, emergency management organizations, and community partners that coordinates emergency preparedness and response activities across the healthcare sector. |
| Utility Company Registry | A voluntary registry maintained by electric and gas utilities identifying customers who are dependent on powered medical equipment and who should receive priority service restoration during outages. |

### 6. Procedures
#### 6.1 Patient Emergency Risk Stratification — Ongoing Maintenance

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned RN | At every SOC assessment, assess the patient's emergency risk level by evaluating all factors in Section 5 — technology dependence, social isolation, medication criticality (refrigeration requirements, infusion medications, injectable medications), mobility and evacuation capability, cognitive impairment affecting self-care decisions, proximity to high-hazard geographic zones (flood plain, wildfire zone, hurricane zone), and caregiver emergency capacity. Assign the patient to Category 1, 2, 3, or 4 and document the assignment and its rationale in the clinical record. | At the SOC assessment; documented within 24 hours. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned RN | At each recertification assessment, reassess and update the patient's emergency risk category. If the patient's category has changed — due to new technology dependence, loss of caregiver support, new clinical complexity, or functional decline — update the EPCP accordingly and document the update. | At each RECERT assessment. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned RN | At each skilled visit, monitor for changes in the patient's emergency risk factors — new equipment added, caregiver illness or unavailability, patient relocation, change in clinical stability. If a change affecting emergency risk category is identified, notify the Director of Nursing within 24 hours and update the category and EPCP as indicated. | At each visit; updates within 24 hours. |
| 6.1.4 | Director of Nursing | Maintain and update the master Patient Emergency Risk Registry — a complete list of all active patients with their assigned risk category, emergency contact information, technology dependence status, and EPCP status — at minimum weekly. The registry shall be accessible to the Director of Nursing and the Administrator at all times, including after business hours, via a secure mobile-accessible format. | Updated weekly; accessible continuously. |
| 6.1.5 | Clinical Coordinator | At a minimum of quarterly, generate the Patient Emergency Risk Registry and review it with the Director of Nursing to verify that all category assignments are current, all EPCPs for Category 1 patients are completed and current, all emergency contact information is verified, and all technology-dependent patients are registered with the relevant utility company's medical baseline or priority program per Section 6.2. | Quarterly review; documented in the Director of Nursing's supervisory log. |

#### 6.2 Technology-Dependent Patient Emergency Planning

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN | For every technology-dependent patient, develop a Technology Failure Contingency Plan as part of the EPCP within 24 hours of the SOC. The plan shall address each powered device the patient uses and shall specify: (a) the clinical consequence of loss of the device; (b) the maximum safe duration the patient can tolerate device failure before clinical deterioration; (c) the backup equipment available in the home (battery backup units, manual alternatives); (d) the emergency actions the patient and caregiver should take if the device fails; (e) the sequence of emergency contacts — agency on-call, equipment vendor emergency line, physician, 911; (f) the preferred evacuation destination if the home environment becomes unsafe. | Within 24 hours of SOC for technology-dependent patients. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN | Assist the patient and caregiver in registering with the local electric utility company's Medical Baseline or Life Support rate program, which provides priority outage notification and, in some utility territories, priority service restoration for customers dependent on powered medical equipment. Document the registration status in the EPCP. Provide the patient with the utility company's emergency contact number. | At the SOC visit for technology-dependent patients; registration confirmed and documented within 14 calendar days. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN | Assist the patient and caregiver in registering with the County Emergency Management Agency's Access and Functional Needs Registry (or equivalent local registry), which identifies vulnerable individuals who may need assistance during evacuations or extended emergencies. Document the registration in the EPCP. | At the SOC visit for Category 1 patients; registration documented within 14 calendar days. |
| 6.2.4 | Assigned RN | Coordinate with the patient's DME vendor to verify: (a) the vendor's emergency response protocol for equipment failures during declared emergencies; (b) the vendor's emergency contact number for after-hours equipment failure; (c) the availability of loaner or replacement equipment during emergencies; (d) battery backup availability for the patient's specific equipment. Document all vendor emergency contact information in the patient's EPCP and in the clinical record. | Within 14 calendar days of SOC for technology-dependent patients. |
| 6.2.5 | Assigned RN | At each visit for a technology-dependent patient, assess and document: (a) the operational status of all powered medical equipment; (b) the adequacy of the power supply (battery backup charge level, electrical supply stability); (c) the patient's and caregiver's demonstrated knowledge of the emergency response sequence for device failure. | At each visit. |

#### 6.3 Emergency Preparedness Care Plan — Development and Maintenance

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN | For every Category 1 and Category 2 patient, develop a written Emergency Preparedness Care Plan (EPCP) using the EPCP Template (Appendix A). The EPCP shall be completed within 48 hours of the SOC visit for Category 1 patients and within 14 calendar days for Category 2 patients. The EPCP shall be incorporated into the plan of care and shall be visible to all treating clinicians in the EHR. | Category 1: within 48 hours of SOC. Category 2: within 14 calendar days of SOC. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | Review the EPCP with the patient and caregiver at the SOC visit and at each recertification assessment. Document the review, the patient's and caregiver's understanding of the emergency plan, and any updates made. | At SOC and each RECERT. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN | Update the EPCP immediately when any of the following occur: (a) the patient acquires or discontinues a powered medical device; (b) the patient's primary caregiver changes; (c) the patient relocates; (d) the patient's clinical status or risk category changes significantly; (e) any element of the EPCP is found to be inaccurate or unworkable. Document all updates in the EHR with the date and reason for the update. | Immediately upon identification of a change. |
| 6.3.4 | Director of Nursing | Review all Category 1 EPCPs monthly to verify currency and completeness. Review all Category 2 EPCPs quarterly. Document the review in the Director of Nursing's supervisory log. | Monthly for Category 1; quarterly for Category 2. |

#### 6.4 Clinical Emergency Response Protocol — Activation and Execution

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Administrator / Director of Nursing | When an emergency event occurs that disrupts or threatens the agency's ability to deliver normal scheduled services — whether or not a formal government declaration has been issued — the Administrator or Director of Nursing shall activate the Clinical Emergency Response Protocol immediately. Activation shall be documented in the Emergency Operations Log (Appendix B) with the date, time, nature of the event, and the name of the activating authority. | Immediately upon identification of an event requiring activation. |
| 6.4.2 | Director of Nursing | Within 1 hour of activation, generate the current Patient Emergency Risk Registry from the EHR. Assign clinical staff to patient contact teams organized by geographic zone and risk category. Establish a clinical command structure: the Director of Nursing serves as the Clinical Emergency Coordinator; an on-call RN is designated for after-hours clinical triage; and a backup RN is identified in case the primary on-call RN is unavailable. Document all assignments in the Emergency Operations Log. | Within 1 hour of activation. |
| 6.4.3 | Assigned Clinical Staff | Execute patient contact per the priority sequence: (a) Category 1 patients — direct telephone or in-person clinical contact within 12 hours of activation; (b) Category 2 patients — telephone contact within 24 hours; (c) Category 3 patients — telephone contact within 48 hours; (d) Category 4 patients — telephone contact within 72 hours. At each contact, assess: the patient's current clinical status; caregiver presence and functioning; equipment status; medication availability and access; immediate safety concerns; and whether a clinical visit is urgently needed. Document each contact attempt and outcome in the Emergency Contact Log (Appendix C) within 4 hours of the contact. | Per category timelines above. |
| 6.4.4 | Assigned Clinical Staff | If a patient cannot be reached by telephone after two attempts with a minimum 30-minute interval between attempts: (a) contact all emergency contacts listed in the clinical record; (b) if the patient is Category 1 or 2 and all contacts are exhausted without success, notify the Director of Nursing immediately; (c) the Director of Nursing shall dispatch a clinician for an in-person welfare check or shall contact local emergency services (fire department welfare check) for the patient's address. Document all contact attempts with dates and times. | Immediately upon identification of an unreachable Category 1 or 2 patient. |
| 6.4.5 | Director of Nursing | Triage clinical visit delivery during the emergency period: (a) determine which patients require urgent in-person visits based on the telephone contact assessments; (b) prioritize in-person visits for patients with active clinical crises, technology failures, or caregiver absence; (c) determine which patients can safely receive telehealth check-ins or telephone clinical triage in lieu of an in-person visit for a defined emergency period; (d) document all triage decisions in the Emergency Operations Log with clinical rationale; (e) notify the physician of any change in visit delivery that departs from the physician-ordered plan of care within 24 hours. | Continuously during the emergency period; physician notification within 24 hours of any plan deviation. |
| 6.4.6 | Director of Nursing | Determine whether the emergency period constitutes a CMS-declared emergency that triggers regulatory flexibilities — such as HIPAA waiver provisions, CoP waiver authority, or emergency billing flexibility under Section 1135 of the Social Security Act. If applicable, notify the Administrator and Compliance Officer immediately. Document the regulatory flexibility determination and any waivers applied. | Within 24 hours of activation. |
| 6.4.7 | Assigned RN | During any emergency-period clinical visit, complete a focused emergency clinical assessment including: (a) full vital signs; (b) medication availability and administration status; (c) equipment operational status; (d) wound care status if applicable; (e) patient's and caregiver's safety, physical wellbeing, and psychological status; (f) adequacy of food, water, and shelter; (g) any immediate medical concerns requiring physician notification or emergency services. Document the emergency-period visit note in the EHR within 24 hours using the standard visit note format with an "Emergency Period Visit" notation. | During each emergency-period visit. |

#### 6.5 Post-Emergency Restoration of Normal Services

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Director of Nursing | As the emergency situation resolves and normal service delivery becomes feasible, restore visit schedules beginning with Category 1 patients and proceeding through Category 4. Document the service restoration plan in the Emergency Operations Log. | As the emergency resolves. |
| 6.5.2 | Assigned RN | Conduct a post-emergency clinical assessment for every patient who experienced a missed or delayed visit during the emergency period. The assessment shall evaluate: any clinical changes that occurred during the disrupted period; medication adherence; equipment status; and the need for any plan of care modifications. Document the post-emergency assessment in the clinical record. | Within 5 business days of service restoration. |
| 6.5.3 | Assigned RN | Notify the physician of any patient who experienced a clinically significant change during the emergency period, including any missed medications, equipment failures, falls, or adverse events. Document the physician notification and the physician's response. | Within 24 hours of the post-emergency assessment. |
| 6.5.4 | Director of Nursing | Conduct the After-Action Review within 30 calendar days of emergency resolution using the After-Action Review Template (Appendix D). Present findings to the QAPI Committee and Administrator. Report to the Governing Body at the next quarterly meeting. | Within 30 calendar days of resolution. |

#### 6.6 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Category 1 patient cannot be reached within 12 hours and all emergency contacts are exhausted | Director of Nursing immediately; 911 if immediate danger suspected | Dispatch an in-person welfare check or contact local fire/police for a welfare check. Document all contact attempts. Physician notification. Incident report per RM-ER-002. | Immediately upon identification. |
| A technology-dependent patient's powered equipment has failed during the emergency | Assigned RN contacts DME vendor emergency line and physician simultaneously | DME vendor dispatches emergency repair or replacement equipment. If patient is in immediate clinical distress, call 911. Document all actions. | Immediately. |
| The agency's clinical staff availability is reduced below the level needed to serve all active patients during the emergency | Director of Nursing and Administrator | Activate mutual aid agreements with neighboring home health agencies per OP-FM-005. Contact Healthcare Coalition for clinical staffing assistance. Prioritize clinical resources to Category 1 and 2 patients only if severe staffing shortage. Notify CMS if the agency cannot fulfill Medicare service obligations. | Within 4 hours of identifying a critical staffing shortage. |
| A patient evacuates without notifying the agency | Clinical Coordinator attempts contact; Director of Nursing notified | Attempt to locate the patient through emergency contacts and the patient's emergency shelter registration if applicable. Document all attempts. If the patient cannot be located within 72 hours, notify the physician and assess for case suspension per CMS emergency guidance. | Contact attempts within 24 hours; Director of Nursing notification within 24 hours. |
| An emergency period visit reveals a patient who has experienced an adverse event during the disrupted service period | Assigned RN contacts physician and Director of Nursing | Physician notification within 1 hour for significant adverse events. Incident report per RM-ER-002. Adverse event report per QA-AE-001 for significant patient harm. Include in After-Action Review. | Physician notification within 1 hour; incident report within 24 hours. |

| Patient Emergency Risk Registry | Master list of all active patients with risk categories and EPCP status | Director of Nursing | EHR — secure administrative module; accessible offline backup | Updated weekly; retained 7 years |
| Emergency Preparedness Care Plan | Individualized EPCP per Appendix A | Assigned RN | EHR — plan of care (Folder 06) | Category 1: within 48 hours of SOC; Category 2: within 14 calendar days; retained 7 years |
| Technology Failure Contingency Plan | Device-specific contingency plan for technology-dependent patients | Assigned RN | EHR — EPCP (within plan of care) | Within 24 hours of SOC for technology-dependent patients; retained 7 years |
| Utility/Registry enrollment documentation | Confirmation of utility medical baseline registration and county emergency registry enrollment | Assigned RN / Clinical Coordinator | EHR — EPCP | Within 14 calendar days of SOC; retained 7 years |

| Emergency Contact Log | Record of all patient contacts during the emergency period with dates, times, outcomes, and clinical assessments | Assigned Clinical Staff | EHR — coordination notes; Emergency Contact Log (Appendix C) | Within 4 hours of each contact; retained 7 years |

| Post-emergency clinical assessment | Assessment of each patient after service restoration | Assigned RN | EHR — visit notes | Within 5 business days of service restoration |

| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment — Appendix E | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days of effective date, revision, or hire |

### 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
#### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All active patients assigned to an emergency risk category at SOC | Chart audit | ≥98% of SOC assessments with documented risk category |
| All Category 1 patients have a completed, current EPCP | EHR audit of Category 1 patient records | ≥98% of Category 1 patients with completed EPCP |
| All technology-dependent patients registered with utility company program | EPCP audit | ≥95% registered or registration actively in progress |
| Patient Emergency Risk Registry updated weekly | Registry audit log | 100% of weeks with documented registry update |
| Emergency contact information current for all active patients | Quarterly chart audit of emergency contact fields | ≥98% with two or more current emergency contacts |
| After-Action Review completed within 30 days of emergency resolution | After-Action Review log | 100% of declared emergencies with After-Action Review |
| All emergency-period patient contacts documented within 4 hours | Emergency Contact Log audit | ≥95% |

#### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors conducting an emergency preparedness survey under the Emergency Preparedness Rule (42 CFR § 484.102) will specifically verify:
Evidence of a risk-based Emergency Operations Plan. The plan must be based on an all-hazards risk assessment for the agency's geographic area. Surveyors will request the EOP and verify it is current, approved by the Governing Body, and tested annually.
Evidence of patient-level emergency planning. Surveyors will select a sample of active patient clinical records and verify that emergency risk categories are documented and that Category 1 and 2 patients have completed EPCPs. The absence of patient-level emergency planning is a frequently cited deficiency.
Evidence that technology-dependent patients have device-specific contingency plans. Surveyors will select patients with powered medical equipment and verify that the EPCP addresses device failure scenarios and that utility company registration has been completed.
Evidence of emergency communications planning. Surveyors will verify that the agency has a communication plan that addresses how patients will be contacted during emergencies and how clinical staff will receive emergency direction.
Evidence of annual training and testing. Surveyors will request training completion records and After-Action Reviews from any emergency events that occurred in the prior year.
Evidence of coordination with community partners. Surveyors will look for documented relationships with the local Healthcare Coalition, county emergency management, and utility providers.
#### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emergency preparedness plan exists at the organizational level but individual patient EPCPs are not completed | CMS deficiency under 42 CFR § 484.102; Category 1 patient left unplanned during emergency | Require EPCP completion as a mandatory element of the SOC workflow; Director of Nursing quarterly audit |
| Technology-dependent patients not registered with utility company's medical baseline program | Patient loses power priority; prolonged outage creates clinical emergency | Assign utility registration as a mandatory action item at SOC for technology-dependent patients; document confirmation |
| Emergency contact information not updated — contacts are outdated at the time of an emergency | Agency cannot reach the patient during the emergency | Verify emergency contacts at each RECERT; Director of Nursing quarterly registry review |
| No After-Action Review conducted following emergency events | Systemic failures not identified; same mistakes recur | Director of Nursing calendar reminder 7 days after emergency resolution; After-Action Review required before QAPI Committee closes the event |
| Emergency-period patient contacts not documented | Survey evidence gap; inability to demonstrate patient welfare was confirmed | Emergency Contact Log required for every contact attempt; Director of Nursing reviews the log daily during emergency activation |

### 10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All clinical staff shall receive initial training on clinical emergency preparedness within 14 calendar days of hire and annually thereafter, covering: the Patient Emergency Risk Stratification System and category criteria; the EPCP development process; technology-dependent patient contingency planning; the Clinical Emergency Response Protocol and priority contact timelines; emergency contact documentation requirements; and the After-Action Review process.
10.2 All on-call and after-hours nursing staff shall receive specific training on emergency activation procedures, Category 1 patient welfare check protocols, and emergency-period clinical triage decision-making.
10.3 Clinical staff shall participate in the agency's annual emergency preparedness drill per RM-EP-002. Clinical participation in the drill shall be documented in each clinician's training record.
10.4 All personnel within scope shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix E) within 14 calendar days of the effective date, any revision, or hire/appointment.
10.5 The Director of Nursing shall maintain training completion records for all clinical staff and shall report any non-compliance to the Administrator within 7 calendar days of any training deadline.
### 11. Version Control
11.1 This policy is maintained under the agency's enterprise policy lifecycle management system per policy EN-LC-001.
11.2 Only the most current approved version of this policy, as reflected in the policy header, is valid for any operational, compliance, or regulatory purpose. All superseded versions must be archived and clearly marked as "SUPERSEDED — NOT FOR USE."
11.3 Any substantive revision to this policy requires: (a) review and approval by the Governing Body, documented in meeting minutes; (b) re-acknowledgment by all personnel within scope within 14 calendar days of the revised effective date; (c) update to the enterprise policy index per EN-TG-001.
11.4 Non-substantive revisions (formatting, typographical corrections, updated cross-references) may be approved by the Administrator with notification to the Governing Body at the next regular meeting.

## CL-PR-006 — Abuse, Neglect & Exploitation Reporting
### 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-PR-006 |
| Policy Title | Abuse, Neglect & Exploitation Reporting |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | PR — Patient Rights & Safety |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

### 2. Purpose
This policy mandates the identification, documentation, reporting, and response to suspected abuse, neglect, and exploitation of patients receiving home health services at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. The home health setting creates a unique and elevated obligation with respect to abuse and neglect reporting. Unlike institutional care settings where multiple eyes observe the patient daily, home health patients are seen intermittently, often in private spaces with only a single caregiver present between visits. The home health clinician may be the only professional to enter the patient's home on a weekly basis — making the clinician the primary sentinel for the identification of abuse, neglect, or exploitation that might otherwise go undetected.
The population served by home health is among the most vulnerable in the healthcare system: elderly patients with cognitive impairment, patients with physical disabilities, pediatric patients, patients with limited social support, and patients who are financially dependent on or emotionally bonded to their caregivers. Perpetrators of elder and dependent adult abuse are frequently family members or paid caregivers — individuals who control the patient's environment, their finances, their medications, and their access to the outside world. A patient who is being abused by a caregiver cannot easily seek help; they may be physically unable to leave the home, cognitively unable to articulate the abuse, emotionally conflicted about reporting a family member, or afraid of retaliation.
California law is unambiguous: every licensed healthcare professional is a mandated reporter under California Penal Code § 11165.7 (for child abuse) and California Welfare and Institutions Code § 15630 (for elder and dependent adult abuse). The reporting obligation is triggered by reasonable suspicion — not proof, not certainty, not a completed investigation. A single bruise in an unusual location, a patient who flinches when a caregiver enters the room, unexplained dehydration, a patient whose prescribed medications are inexplicably missing, an elder whose bank accounts are being drained — any of these may constitute grounds for a mandated report. This policy establishes the complete framework for recognizing, reporting, documenting, and following up on suspected abuse, neglect, and exploitation, consistent with California mandated reporting law and the agency's obligations under 42 CFR § 484.50 (Patient Rights) and CMS conditions for patient abuse-free care.
### 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All agency personnel — every individual employed by or contracted with Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. who has any contact with patients or who becomes aware of information suggesting abuse, neglect, or exploitation of a patient. This explicitly includes: all clinical disciplines (RN, LVN, PT, OT, SLP, MSW, HHA); intake staff; scheduling staff; administrative staff; and contracted clinical staff.
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager
The Compliance Officer who oversees reporting compliance and investigation coordination
The Administrator who bears organizational accountability for patient rights protection
Human Resources — for situations where the alleged abuser is an agency employee
This policy applies to every patient served by Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc., regardless of age — including adult patients, elderly patients, dependent adults, and pediatric patients (for whom the separate mandatory reporting standard under California Penal Code § 11165.7 also applies).
### 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. shall maintain a comprehensive abuse, neglect, and exploitation prevention, identification, and reporting program that ensures every patient receives care in an environment free from all forms of abuse, neglect, exploitation, and misappropriation of property.
4.2 Every employee and contractor of Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. who has any contact with patients is a mandated reporter under California law and is personally, professionally, and legally obligated to report known or reasonably suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of: (a) patients under age 18 — to law enforcement or the California Department of Social Services child protective services per California Penal Code § 11165.7 and § 11166; (b) patients aged 18 or older who are elders (age 65 or older) or dependent adults — to Adult Protective Services (APS) or the local law enforcement agency per California Welfare and Institutions Code § 15630.
4.3 The reporting obligation is triggered by reasonable suspicion alone — without requiring proof, confirmation, investigation findings, or supervisor approval. A mandated reporter who observes or becomes aware of information that would lead a reasonable person to suspect abuse, neglect, or exploitation is required by law to report. The failure to report when reasonable suspicion exists is a criminal misdemeanor under California law.
4.4 The mandated reporter's obligation is individual and personal — it cannot be delegated to a supervisor, transferred to the agency, or satisfied by notifying the Director of Nursing. Notifying the Director of Nursing is required by this policy and is an important organizational step — but it does not fulfill the individual reporter's personal legal obligation to report to the appropriate government authority.
4.5 The agency shall not discourage, obstruct, delay, or retaliate against any individual who makes a mandated report in good faith, regardless of whether the report is subsequently substantiated. Retaliation against a mandated reporter is a violation of California law, agency policy CO-CP-005, and the patient rights protections of 42 CFR § 484.50.
4.6 No employee or contractor of the agency shall investigate suspected abuse independently, confront the suspected abuser, or take any action that could compromise the investigation being conducted by the appropriate government agency. The agency's role is to report, to ensure the patient's immediate safety, and to cooperate with the investigating authority — not to conduct an independent investigation.
4.7 When the alleged or suspected abuser is a person employed by or contracted through the agency — including any HHA, clinical staff member, intake staff, or other agency personnel — the Director of Nursing shall immediately remove that individual from patient contact pending investigation, and the Compliance Officer shall be notified within 2 hours to coordinate the agency's response.
4.8 Any patient who has been or is suspected of being abused, neglected, or exploited shall receive a prompt clinical assessment of their safety and healthcare needs, and the agency shall take all clinically appropriate steps to ensure the patient's safety — including coordination with APS, law enforcement, or other protective authorities — while maintaining the patient's dignity and respecting their rights.
4.9 The agency shall document all observations, reports, patient assessments, contacts with government agencies, and follow-up actions related to every suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation situation in the patient's clinical record and in the agency's Incident Report and Compliance Investigation files.
### 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Abuse | The willful infliction of injury, unreasonable confinement, intimidation, or punishment with resulting physical harm, pain, or mental anguish. In the home health context, abuse may be physical, verbal/emotional, sexual, or financial. |
| Physical Abuse | The intentional use of force against a patient that results in bodily injury, pain, or impairment — including hitting, slapping, pushing, restraining, or use of physical force in any form. |
| Verbal / Emotional Abuse | The use of demeaning, threatening, intimidating, humiliating, or psychologically harmful language or actions directed at a patient — including yelling, cursing, threats, and deliberate acts of humiliation. |
| Sexual Abuse | Non-consensual sexual contact of any kind, including any sexual contact with an individual who lacks the cognitive capacity to consent. |
| Financial Exploitation | The illegal or improper use of a patient's funds, property, or financial resources without the patient's knowledge or valid consent — including theft, fraud, misappropriation of funds, unauthorized use of accounts, and coerced changes to estate documents. |
| Neglect | The failure to provide adequate care, supervision, or protection to a patient by a caregiver who has responsibility for the patient's welfare — including failure to provide food, water, shelter, clothing, medical care, medication, or personal hygiene assistance. Self-neglect — when a patient refuses care — is not the same as caregiver neglect and is addressed through clinical education and documentation, not mandated reporting. |
| Self-Neglect | The failure of a patient to provide for their own essential needs due to cognitive impairment, mental illness, or personal choice. Distinguished from caregiver neglect; addressed through clinical and social work intervention, not mandated reporting. |
| Abandonment | The desertion of a patient by a person who has assumed responsibility for providing care, when that person walks away without arranging for alternative care. |
| Misappropriation of Property | The deliberate misplacement, exploitation, or wrongful, temporary, or permanent use of a patient's belongings or property without the patient's knowledge or consent. |
| Reasonable Suspicion | A belief, based on specific articulable facts and reasonable inferences drawn from those facts, that would lead a reasonable person in a similar position to conclude that a patient may have been subjected to abuse, neglect, or exploitation. Reasonable suspicion does not require proof and does not require the reporter to have personally witnessed the abuse. |
| Elder | Under California Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.27, any person who is 65 years of age or older. |
| Dependent Adult | Under California Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.23, any person between the ages of 18 and 64 who has physical or mental limitations that restrict their ability to carry out normal activities or to protect their rights, including persons with physical or developmental disabilities, or cognitive impairment. |
| Mandated Reporter | Under California law, any person designated by statute who is required to report known or reasonably suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of specified vulnerable populations. All licensed healthcare professionals are mandated reporters. |
| Adult Protective Services (APS) | The California county agency responsible for investigating reports of abuse, neglect, and exploitation of elders and dependent adults. APS hotlines are available 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. In California, the statewide APS reporting line is available through each county; a consolidated reporting resource is available at 1-833-401-0832. |
| Child Protective Services (CPS) | The California county agency responsible for investigating reports of child abuse and neglect. Reports may be made to the local CPS office or to law enforcement. California's statewide CPS reporting resource: 1-800-540-4000. |
| Inflicted Injury | An injury that is inconsistent with the explanation provided, inconsistent with the patient's developmental or physical capabilities, in an unusual anatomical location, or in multiple stages of healing suggesting repeated incidents. |
| Non-Accidental Trauma | Physical injury resulting from intentional force rather than accident, fall, or medical condition — determined by pattern, location, severity, and consistency with the explanation provided. |

### 6. Procedures
#### 6.1 Recognition — Indicators of Abuse, Neglect, and Exploitation
All agency personnel shall be trained to recognize the following indicators of potential abuse, neglect, or exploitation. The presence of one or more of these indicators, particularly in the absence of a plausible clinical or accidental explanation, constitutes a basis for reasonable suspicion and triggers the reporting obligation.
6.1.1 Physical Abuse Indicators:
Unexplained bruising, welts, lacerations, or burns — particularly in locations unusual for accidental injury (torso, upper arms, posterior trunk, genitalia, buttocks)
Bilateral injuries (both sides of the body) suggesting deliberate force rather than accidental fall
Multiple injuries in different stages of healing
Injuries with a pattern consistent with an object (belt buckle shape, cord marks, hand prints)
Delay between injury occurrence and medical treatment
Explanation of injury inconsistent with the injury's nature, severity, or the patient's physical capabilities
Patient or caregiver appears anxious, rehearsed, or inconsistent when explaining an injury
Patient flinches, cowers, or shows extreme anxiety in the presence of the caregiver
6.1.2 Verbal/Emotional Abuse Indicators:
Patient appears fearful, withdrawn, depressed, or agitated in the caregiver's presence but calmer when the caregiver is absent
Caregiver uses demeaning, threatening, or infantilizing language toward the patient in the clinician's presence
Patient exhibits new behavioral changes including social withdrawal, loss of appetite, or regression
Patient expresses fear of the caregiver or fear of what will happen to them after the clinician leaves
Patient is not allowed to speak privately with the clinician or to communicate without the caregiver present and monitoring
6.1.3 Sexual Abuse Indicators:
Unexplained injuries or trauma to the genital or rectal areas
Presence of sexually transmitted infection with no identified source
Unexplained bleeding from vaginal or rectal areas
Sexually inappropriate behaviors newly exhibited by a patient with cognitive impairment
Patient's report, even partial or confused, of unwanted sexual contact
6.1.4 Financial Exploitation Indicators:
Unpaid bills or utilities despite apparent adequate income
Sudden changes in bank account activity, account ownership, or beneficiary designations
Unexplained disappearance of funds, assets, or personal property from the home
Caregiver shows unusual interest in the patient's finances, insists on controlling all financial transactions, or prevents the patient from accessing their own money
Patient is not receiving adequate food, clothing, or medical care despite financial resources
New or unexplained changes to wills, powers of attorney, or property titles
Patient reports that personal belongings or money are missing
6.1.5 Neglect Indicators:
Patient is dehydrated, malnourished, or losing weight without a medical explanation
Patient has untreated injuries, infections, or medical conditions
Patient lacks adequate food, water, medications, or basic personal care supplies despite caregiver responsibility
Patient's living environment is extremely unsafe, unsanitary, or inadequate (no heat, no food, animal waste in the patient's care area)
The caregiver is consistently absent or fails to provide ordered care
Patient's medications are missing or not being administered
Patient has developed pressure injuries that are inconsistent with the level of care they should be receiving
6.1.6 Exploitation and Misappropriation Indicators:
Personal belongings or valuables missing from the patient's home between visits
Caregiver admits to borrowing money or property from the patient
Patient reports giving money or valuables to the caregiver
HHA or other staff member is found to possess items belonging to the patient
#### 6.2 Immediate Response Upon Identifying Suspected Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Any Agency Personnel | If a staff member observes or becomes aware of information that creates reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect, or exploitation — whether during a visit, during an intake call, during a scheduling contact, or through any other means — do not investigate independently, do not confront the suspected abuser, and do not discuss the suspicion with anyone other than the Director of Nursing and the Compliance Officer. | Immediately upon forming reasonable suspicion. |
| 6.2.2 | Any Agency Personnel | If the patient is in immediate danger during the visit — if there is an immediate risk of physical harm from a present individual — call 911 immediately and notify the Director of Nursing. Ensure the patient's immediate safety by remaining present until law enforcement arrives or the immediate threat is resolved. | Immediately. 911 is always the first call when there is immediate danger. |
| 6.2.3 | Any Agency Personnel | Conduct a discrete clinical assessment of the patient's condition — document all injuries, the patient's statements, the caregiver's statements, and your clinical observations with objective specificity. Do not alter, clean, or photograph injuries in a way that could disturb evidence. If photographing injuries is clinically indicated (for wound care documentation), follow the standard wound photography protocol per CL-SD-011 and note in the clinical record that the photographs were taken for documentation purposes. | During the visit; as clinically appropriate. |
| 6.2.4 | Any Agency Personnel | Notify the Director of Nursing within 2 hours of forming reasonable suspicion. This notification does not fulfill the individual mandated reporting obligation — it is an organizational notification required by this policy. The individual reporter retains their personal legal obligation to make a mandated report. | Within 2 hours. |
| 6.2.5 | Identifying Staff Member | Make a verbal mandated report to the appropriate government authority: (a) For patients age 65 or older or dependent adults age 18–64: report to the local county Adult Protective Services (APS) agency — reachable 24/7 — or to local law enforcement. California APS resource: 1-833-401-0832 or the local county APS number; (b) For patients under age 18: report to the local county Child Protective Services (CPS) — reachable 24/7 — or to local law enforcement. California CPS resource: 1-800-540-4000. The verbal report shall include: the reporter's name and contact information (reporters are legally protected from disclosure of their identity unless they consent); the patient's name and address; the nature and extent of the suspected abuse or neglect; the basis for the reasonable suspicion; and any other information that may be helpful to the investigation. | Verbal report immediately upon forming reasonable suspicion; must be made by the individual reporter regardless of supervisor notification. |
| 6.2.6 | Identifying Staff Member | For adult abuse (APS reports): A written confirmation report — Form SOC 341 (Report of Suspected Dependent Adult/Elder Abuse) — must be submitted to the reporting county within 2 working days of the initial verbal report. Retain a copy of the written report in the agency's compliance file. | Within 2 working days of the verbal report. |
| 6.2.7 | Identifying Staff Member | For child abuse (CPS reports): A written Suspected Child Abuse Report — Form SS 8572 — must be submitted within 36 hours of the initial verbal report. Retain a copy of the written report in the agency's compliance file. | Within 36 hours of the verbal report. |
| 6.2.8 | Director of Nursing | Notify the Compliance Officer within 2 hours of the Director of Nursing's notification. Notify the Administrator within 4 hours. | Within 2 hours for Compliance Officer; within 4 hours for Administrator. |

#### 6.3 Patient Safety Assessment and Clinical Follow-Up

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN / Director of Nursing | Conduct a comprehensive clinical assessment of the patient's current health status to identify and address any healthcare needs resulting from the suspected abuse or neglect — including injury assessment, nutritional status, medication status, and psychological wellbeing. Document all findings in the clinical record with objective clinical language. | Within 24 hours of the initial report or as soon as safe access to the patient is established. |
| 6.3.2 | Director of Nursing | Assess the patient's immediate safety situation: (a) Is the suspected abuser present in the home? (b) Is the patient in a safe environment? (c) Does the patient require immediate protective action (placement in a safe location, law enforcement intervention)? Document the safety assessment and the actions taken. | Within 24 hours; immediately if the patient's safety is at immediate risk. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN / MSW | Coordinate with APS, CPS, or law enforcement to support the investigation as requested by the investigating authority, including providing clinical information within the bounds of HIPAA and mandatory reporting law. Refer the patient to the MSW for psychosocial assessment and community resource coordination per CL-SD-005. | During and after the investigation as requested. |
| 6.3.4 | Director of Nursing / Assigned RN | Increase visit frequency for the affected patient as clinically indicated and as feasible, to enhance monitoring of the patient's safety and wellbeing during the investigation period. Obtain physician orders for any increase in visit frequency. | Within 48 hours of the initial report. |
| 6.3.5 | Assigned RN | At each visit following a mandated report, continue to assess for additional signs of abuse, neglect, or exploitation and document clinical findings with objective specificity. If new indicators are identified, make a new mandated report — the initial report does not cover subsequent events. | At each subsequent visit. |
| 6.3.6 | Director of Nursing | Notify the physician of the suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation and of the mandated report made, within 24 hours. Obtain physician guidance on any clinical modifications needed for the patient's care. Document the physician notification. | Within 24 hours of the initial report. |

#### 6.4 When the Alleged Abuser Is an Agency Employee or Contractor

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Director of Nursing | If the suspected abuser is any person employed by or contracted through the agency — including any HHA, clinical staff member, administrative staff, or contracted clinician — remove that individual from all patient contact immediately upon the Director of Nursing becoming aware of the suspicion. Do not wait for confirmation before removing the individual from patient contact. | Immediately upon identification. |
| 6.4.2 | Director of Nursing / Compliance Officer | Notify the Compliance Officer within 2 hours. The Compliance Officer shall initiate a compliance investigation per CO-CP-007 in parallel with the government's mandatory investigation. The agency's internal investigation shall not interfere with or impede the government investigation. | Within 2 hours. |
| 6.4.3 | HR Director / Compliance Officer | Place the suspected employee on administrative leave with or without pay per HR-ER-002, pending the outcome of the investigation. The HR Director and Administrator shall determine the employment disposition once the investigation is complete. | Immediately upon identification. |
| 6.4.4 | Compliance Officer | Assess whether the agency is required to report the suspected employee to the applicable licensing board (California Board of Registered Nursing; Physical Therapy Board of California; etc.) — most California professional licensing boards require reporting of employees who have been found to have committed abuse of a vulnerable adult. File the required board report within the applicable statutory timeframe. | Within the applicable statutory timeframe upon substantiation. |
| 6.4.5 | Director of Nursing | Assign a replacement clinician to the affected patient immediately to ensure continuity of care during the investigation. | Immediately upon removing the suspected employee. |
| 6.4.6 | Compliance Officer | Report the incident to the Governing Body at the next quarterly meeting, or sooner if the incident is of sufficient severity. Include the investigation outcome and any corrective actions taken. | At the next quarterly meeting or as soon as clinically and operationally appropriate. |

#### 6.5 Documentation Requirements for All Abuse-Related Situations

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Identifying Staff Member | Document all clinical observations, patient statements, caregiver statements, and clinical findings in the patient's clinical record using objective, factual language — not interpretive or accusatory. Document what you observed, what you heard, and what you assessed — not conclusions about guilt or innocence. Example of appropriate documentation: "Observed a 4 cm x 2 cm ecchymosis on the right inner forearm, yellowish-green in color consistent with an injury approximately 5–7 days old. Patient stated 'he hit me' when asked about the bruise. Caregiver (patient's adult son) was present in the room." | In the visit note, within 24 hours; the clinical record is the primary legal document. |
| 6.5.2 | Identifying Staff Member | Document the mandated report separately in the Abuse/Neglect Reporting Log (Appendix A): date and time of verbal report; agency contacted; case number assigned by the agency; name of the APS/CPS/law enforcement contact; date of written report submission; and any follow-up actions received from the government agency. | At the time of each action; retained per CO-HP-007. |
| 6.5.3 | Director of Nursing | Document the Director of Nursing's safety assessment, all actions taken to ensure the patient's safety, all physician notifications, and all coordination with APS/CPS/law enforcement in the clinical record's care coordination notes. | Within 24 hours of the Director of Nursing's involvement. |
| 6.5.4 | Compliance Officer | File the complete mandatory reporting package in the agency's Compliance Investigation file: copies of the verbal report documentation, the written mandatory report (SOC 341 or SS 8572), all clinical documentation, all internal investigation findings, all government agency communications, and the final resolution. | Retained per CO-HP-007 — minimum 7 years. |

#### 6.6 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A clinician states they are not certain enough to report — "I'm not sure if this is really abuse" | Director of Nursing | Remind the clinician that California law requires reporting on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. Walk through the clinical observations together. If reasonable suspicion exists, the report must be made. The Director of Nursing can support the clinician in making the call but cannot take over the individual's reporting obligation. | Immediately. |
| A supervisor instructs a staff member not to make a mandated report | That staff member should immediately contact the Compliance Officer | The Compliance Officer shall make the report on behalf of the agency and shall initiate a compliance investigation into the supervisor's conduct. The supervisor's instruction is an illegal obstruction of a mandated report under California law. | Immediately; report cannot be delayed. |
| The patient denies the abuse and refuses protective intervention | Assigned RN and MSW | The patient's denial does not eliminate the mandated reporting obligation — reasonable suspicion triggers the report regardless of the patient's statement. Document the patient's denial. Assist the patient in understanding their options without pressure. APS or CPS will conduct their investigation independently. | Report made; patient's denial documented. |
| An APS investigator arrives at the patient's home during an agency visit | Assigned Clinician | Cooperate fully with the investigation. Provide access to the patient. Provide clinical information to the investigator within the bounds of mandatory reporting law (which creates a permitted disclosure under HIPAA in this context). Document the investigator's visit in the clinical record. | During the investigator's visit. |
| An agency employee is found to have failed to make a mandated report when reasonable suspicion was present | Director of Nursing and Compliance Officer | The agency shall make the report immediately if not yet made. The Compliance Officer shall initiate a compliance investigation into the failure to report. The HR Director shall assess the employment consequences. The failure to report may constitute a criminal misdemeanor under California Penal Code § 11166. | Immediate report; investigation within 24 hours. |

### 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
#### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All mandated reporters complete annual mandatory reporting training | Training completion records per HR-TD-001 | 100% of all agency personnel complete training annually |
| Verbal mandated reports made immediately upon reasonable suspicion | Abuse/Neglect Reporting Log audit | 100% — zero incidents of delayed reporting where reasonable suspicion was present |
| Written mandatory reports submitted within required statutory timeframes | Reporting Log audit comparing verbal and written report dates | 100% — zero late written reports |
| Patients suspected of abuse receive clinical assessment within 24 hours | Director of Nursing review log | ≥95% |
| All employee abuse incidents result in immediate removal from patient contact | HR file audit | 100% |
| Compliance Investigation file complete for every reported incident | Compliance Officer file audit | 100% |

#### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors under Tag G167 through Tag G177 (42 CFR § 484.50) will specifically verify:
Evidence of a zero-tolerance abuse policy. Surveyors will request the agency's abuse policy and will evaluate whether it clearly prohibits all forms of abuse and provides specific reporting requirements.
Evidence of annual abuse awareness and mandatory reporting training. Surveyors will request training records for all staff. A staff member who cannot describe what constitutes abuse, the mandatory reporting threshold, or the reporting process is a training deficiency citation.
Evidence that the agency takes prompt action when abuse is suspected. Surveyors may review clinical records and incident reports to verify that identified abuse indicators triggered reports and patient safety assessments. They will look for patterns where abuse indicators were documented in clinical records without corresponding mandatory reports.
Evidence that employees suspected of abuse are immediately removed from patient contact. Surveyors will review any incidents involving suspected employee abuse and verify the agency's response timeline.
Interview patients and caregivers about whether they feel safe and whether they know how to report concerns about their care.
Evidence that the non-retaliation policy is operational. Surveyors may ask staff members whether they know they are protected from retaliation for making a report.
#### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staff believe they need to be certain before reporting — waiting for "proof" | Delayed reporting; failure to fulfill mandatory reporting obligation; criminal liability for the individual | Annual training emphasizing the reasonable suspicion standard; Director of Nursing open-door policy for staff with concerns |
| Clinical records document injury indicators without corresponding mandatory report documentation | Survey citation; pattern of unreported abuse | Director of Nursing monthly chart audit cross-referencing injury notations with the Abuse/Neglect Reporting Log |
| Supervisor intercepts staff reports and decides at the supervisor level not to report | Illegal obstruction; organizational liability | Training that explicitly teaches all staff their individual, personal, non-delegable reporting obligation; Compliance hotline available for direct employee reporting |
| Written mandatory report not submitted within required timeframe after verbal report | Legal non-compliance; possible criminal liability | Reporting Log includes written report due date field; Compliance Officer audits timeliness quarterly |
| No follow-up clinical assessment after a mandated report | Patient safety failure; survey deficiency | Director of Nursing assigns follow-up assessment as a mandatory action item upon notification |

### 10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All agency personnel — including every clinical discipline, intake staff, scheduling staff, and administrative staff — shall receive initial training on mandatory abuse reporting within 14 calendar days of hire. This training shall be specifically validated as complete by signature — acknowledgment of this policy satisfies the written attestation requirement under California Penal Code § 11166.5 for child abuse mandated reporters.
10.2 Annual refresher training on mandatory abuse reporting shall be completed by all agency personnel before the anniversary of their hire date. The Director of Nursing shall report any training non-compliance to the Administrator within 7 calendar days of any training deadline.
10.3 Annual training shall include: the definitions of abuse, neglect, exploitation, and misappropriation; the specific clinical indicators for each type; the reasonable suspicion standard; the personal, individual, non-delegable nature of the reporting obligation; the verbal and written report requirements and timelines; the identity of the reporting authorities and their contact information; the non-retaliation protection; and the consequences for failure to report.
10.4 Scenario-based training using realistic home health clinical situations shall be incorporated into the annual training to ensure that clinicians can recognize abuse indicators in practice — not just in the abstract.
10.5 All personnel within scope shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix B) within 14 calendar days of the effective date, any revision, or hire/appointment. This acknowledgment also satisfies the California Penal Code § 11166.5 written statement requirement confirming the employee's knowledge of mandatory child abuse reporting obligations.
### 11. Version Control
11.1 This policy is maintained under the agency's enterprise policy lifecycle management system per policy EN-LC-001.
11.2 Only the most current approved version of this policy is valid for any operational, compliance, or regulatory purpose. All superseded versions must be archived and clearly marked as "SUPERSEDED — NOT FOR USE."
11.3 Any substantive revision requires: (a) review and approval by the Governing Body, documented in meeting minutes; (b) re-acknowledgment by all personnel within scope within 14 calendar days; (c) update to the enterprise policy index per EN-TG-001.
11.4 Non-substantive revisions may be approved by the Administrator with Governing Body notification at the next regular meeting.
